blocks.h: THE LONGEST NIGHT, THE EARTH SAID
Roya Publication No. 111
by Chew Z
SYNOPSIS

Bam is a green town at the edge of the hottest desert on Earth, a sea of date palms and orange groves in the southeast of Iran, kept alive for a thousand years by water carried under the sand in hand-dug tunnels. Above it, on a rock, stands the Arg, a whole city made of mud, the largest building of earth anywhere in the world.

Ayoub makes the bricks. He treads the mud with his bare feet the way his father did, and lays it into the old walls of the Arg where the years have worn them away. In the evenings he smokes a little opium, as men in his province do, and watches his daughter Narges read Hafez by lamplight. She is sixteen, she wants to translate the great poet into English, and last summer her father built her a modern room of her own, with a flat concrete roof.

Clara has come from Germany to see the Arg. She repairs old buildings made of clay, and she has come alone, at Christmas, because her father has just died and asked her to go and see something. On the longest night of the year, Yalda, Narges invites her home, and opens the book of Hafez to read the stranger her fortune.
It is December 2003. Every day from now on will be longer. That’s the whole point.
On Christmas night, the ground clears its throat.
And in the gaps between the chapters, something very old, which everyone in this book has walked on all their lives, has started to speak.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
This book is fiction wrapped around something that happened.

At twenty-six minutes past five on the morning of December 26, 2003, an earthquake broke under the town of Bam, in Kerman province in southeastern Iran. It lasted about twelve seconds. It destroyed nearly every building in the city, brought down the ancient earthen citadel of Arg-e Bam, and killed something above thirty thousand people. The exact number was never settled. Most of the town’s hospitals, clinics, fire stations and police stations fell with everyone inside them, and for the first day the people of Bam dug each other out with their hands. The world came afterwards, with dogs and machines, from forty countries, including, for the first time in more than twenty years, American military planes.

I have tried to keep the order of events, the weather, the scale and the broad findings of the scientists and engineers faithful to the public record: the two foreshocks the evening before and the third before dawn; the rupture on a hidden branch of a fault that ran under the city rather than where the maps had it; the unusually violent upward shaking; the collapse of buildings both old and new, and the particular deadliness of heavy concrete roofs that were not tied to their walls; the building code written after the earthquake at Tabas and not enforced; the slow call for outside help; the tents and the prefabricated boxes; the mass graves marked with photographs; the rise in opium use among the survivors; and the long, patient rebuilding of the citadel in mud brick by hand. Because this is a story and not a report, I have kept the numbers loose and some of the times approximate.
Everyone in this book is invented: Ayoub, Tahereh, Narges and Clara, and everyone around them. No real survivor’s story is told here under their name.

The theories in this book belong to its characters and to the earth that speaks between the chapters. I have tried to set them out fairly, the plausible ones beside the impossible ones, and then, because more than twenty years have passed, to say plainly what became of each. Some were true. Some were partly true. One, the secret bomb, was not true at all, and still returns after every earthquake in Iran. I have tried not to point at anyone. The earth doesn’t, and I am not sure I have the right.

The voice in the dark is the one thing in this book I have bent. Many people buried after earthquakes have reported hearing voices, and there are good, plain, physical reasons for it, which the book gives. I have not decided what Clara heard. Neither has she.

The poem is real. Yusof-e gomgashteh, Lost Joseph, is one of the best-loved ghazals of Hafez of Shiraz, who died more than six hundred years ago, and Iranians really do open his book at random on the longest night of the year to read their fortunes in it. The translations here are my own, and like Narges’s, they are a stranger wearing his coat.
This book is for the people of Bam.
Chew Z
I. THE LONGEST NIGHT
1. Mud and Straw Ayoub

My name is Ayoub [a-YOOB]. It is our name for Job, the man in the old holy books whom God tested by taking away everything he had: his flocks, his house, his health, and his children, who died when a great wind brought the roof of their house down on them while they ate. In Persian, when somebody suffers a long time without complaining, we say they have sabr-e Ayoub [SABR-eh a-YOOB], the patience of Job. My mother chose the name because she had waited six years for a son, and she said that by the end she had needed the patience of Ayoub herself. I have always thought it was a heavy name to give a baby. You should not name a child after a man whose children died under a roof.

I make bricks out of mud. I want to tell you that plainly at the beginning, because it is the most important thing about me and also the least impressive, and people who hear it nod politely and look for someone else to talk to.

Here is how it is done. You take the earth of Bam [BAM], which is fine and pale and the colour of a camel, and you wet it, and you let it rest overnight so the water goes all the way into it. In the morning you tread it with your bare feet, the way they used to tread grapes in the old stories, until it is soft as dough. You mix in straw, chopped short, so the brick has bones. Then you press the mud into a wooden frame on the ground, lift the frame away, and there is a brick, lying in the sun. In three weeks of Bam sun it is hard as bone. We call it khesht [KHESHT]. My father made khesht, and his father, and his father, back further than anyone bothered to count, and every one of them lived in houses built of it and was buried in ground that was the same stuff before they shaped it.

That is the whole secret of my trade. A khesht is earth that has agreed, for a while, to be a wall. When it is finished being a wall, it goes back to being earth. It does not argue. It has no pride. I have always liked that about it.
But there is another trade in my blood, and I should tell you about it now, because it runs under this whole story the way the water runs under Bam.

My mother’s father was a muqanni [mo-GHAN-nee]. A qanat [gha-NAAT] digger. I will explain what a qanat is soon, properly, because nobody can understand my town without it. For now it is enough to know that it is a tunnel under the desert that carries water, and that a muqanni is the man who goes down into the earth to dig it and to keep it clean, by hand, with a short pick and a lamp, in a passage hardly wider than his shoulders, a hundred metres underground. My grandfather did that work for forty years. The muqanni have a name for the qanat, among themselves. They call it qātel [ghaa-TEL]. The murderer. They pray before they go down. They will not go down on days they think are unlucky. And they wear white, so that if the earth closes over them, they are already dressed for the grave.

In the spring of the year I was born, a tunnel came down on my grandfather a few kilometres south of the old citadel. His partners dug for two days and brought him up the shaft on a rope, in his white shirt, which was brown. My mother was nursing me when they carried him past the door. She made my father swear on the Qur’an, that same night, that their son would work on top of the earth and never inside it.

So I make bricks. Above the earth, not under it. My father kept his oath. But when I was nine, my grandfather’s old partner, an old man with one blind eye and hands like tree roots, who missed the dead man and had no sons of his own, took me down a shaft one summer afternoon without telling anybody, and sat me at the bottom beside the water, and began to teach me. He taught me for six summers. My mother never knew. I kept that secret for more than forty years. I am telling you because I promised to leave nothing out, and because, at the bottom of everything that happens in this story, there is a qanat.
Let me show you where I lived, because it is not there anymore in the way I am going to describe it, and somebody should keep it.

Bam is a town in the southeast of Iran, in the province of Kerman [ker-MAAN], at the edge of a desert called the Lut [LOOT]. The Lut is one of the hottest places on Earth. Scientists in America once measured the ground there from a satellite, and it read seventy degrees, hot enough to cook an egg on a stone in a minute, and they did not believe it, and they measured again, and it read the same. Nothing lives in the middle of the Lut. Not a lizard. Not a fly. Only wind and sand and black stones, and dunes as tall as mountains, and at night a silence so big you can hear your own blood.

The climate of Bam is the climate of that edge. In summer the heat comes in off the Lut like the breath of an oven with its door left open, forty-five degrees in the shade, fifty some days, and the wind carries a fine grey dust that gets into your teeth and your bread and the folds of your clothes, and the old people sit in the cellars in the afternoons and do not come up until the sun is gone. It hardly rains. A few times a year, a few centimetres, and the whole town comes out into the lanes to smell it. And in winter, which nobody believes about a desert, the nights are cold. The sky is so clear that the day’s heat goes straight up out of the ground into the stars, and by morning there is frost on the water in the pools and ice on the palm fronds, and you can see your breath in your own kitchen. Bam lives between those two, the oven and the frost, and always has.

And on the edge of that nothing, there is Bam. A green place. Palm trees, millions of them, standing in their groves like a crowd waiting for a parade. Orange orchards. Walls of mud around the gardens, and the gardens cool and dark inside, with water running along little channels at the foot of the trees. Coming to Bam across the desert is like coming out of a fever into a cool room. Travellers have been saying so for a thousand years.
The green is made by water, and the water comes from under the ground, and I will tell you about that, because nobody can understand Bam without it. But first I want to tell you about the dates.

Bam’s dates are called mazāfati [ma-zaa-fa-TEE]. They are black, and soft, and so sweet and wet that you cannot dry them; you have to keep them cool or they melt into themselves. My grandmother said a good Bam date tastes like honey that has been sad for a long time and has finally been forgiven. She said things like that. In the autumn the whole town smells of them, of sugar and dust, and men climb the palms with a rope round their waists and their feet bare, and cut the great heavy clusters, and lower them down to the women on the ground, and everybody’s hands are sticky until winter.
Above all of this, on a low rock at the edge of the old town, stands the Arg [ARG].

Arg means citadel, a fortress. The Arg-e Bam [ARG-eh BAM] is a whole city made of mud. Not a building. A city. Walls a mile around, with thirty-eight towers on them. Inside the walls, streets and houses and a bazaar and a mosque and stables and a bathhouse and a school, all of it built of khesht and plastered with kāhgel [kaah-GEL], which is mud mixed with straw and smoothed over the walls like butter on bread. And at the top, on the highest point of the rock, the governor’s castle, rising in terraces one above another, its high walls and its square tower against the sky.

People say the Arg is two thousand years old. That is the kind of thing people say. The truth is that it has been built and broken and rebuilt so many times that it is all ages at once: some of the walls are old as the Silk Road, which ran right past our gate, and some I made myself, in 1998, with my own feet in the mud. It was the biggest building made of earth anywhere in the world. Scholars came from Japan and Italy and Germany to stand in front of it and take measurements and argue with each other in English.

At sunset the whole Arg turns colour. It goes gold first, then a deep orange like the inside of an apricot, then red, then for a few minutes a strange soft violet, and then the light goes out of it all at once and it is just a dark shape on the sky, with the first stars coming out over the towers. I have seen that maybe ten thousand times. I never once got tired of it. That is the truth.

The Arg has seen everything, and remembered it in its walls. Caravans on the Silk Road stopped under it for a thousand years, camels by the hundred with bells round their necks, carrying silk and indigo and spices from India and China toward the west, and the merchants slept inside its walls and paid the governor for the privilege. Armies came for it. Seljuk [sel-JOOK] Turks took it and built it higher. Afghans came over the desert and besieged it. In

1795 the last prince of the Zand [ZAND] kings, beaten everywhere else, ran here with what was left of his men and made his last stand behind these walls, and was betrayed at the gate, and handed over to the man who would found the next dynasty. Then, about a hundred and sixty years ago, the people slowly moved out, down off the rock into the new town among the palms, and left the old city to the pigeons and the wind. It stood empty above us all my life, a whole town with nobody in it, like a ship that everyone has left and that will not sink.

I worked there. For eleven years I was on the restoration crew for the Arg, making khesht to the old recipe and laying it into the old walls where the rain and the years had eaten them. The government paid us, not much, and late. I would have done it for less. My father said a man who makes bricks for the Arg is making bricks for the dead and the unborn at the same time, and that it is the only honest work in Iran.

I had a wife, Tahereh [taa-heh-REH], who was cleverer than me and pretended not to be, for my sake, which is a kindness I only understood after twenty years. My mother had died some years before, and so there were only the three of us in the house. Tahereh and I slept in the oldest room of the house, a room with a domed roof made of khesht that my grandfather built. And I had a daughter. One daughter. Narges [nar-GES].

Narges is the narcissus flower. It is the only flower that blooms in our winter. Out in the fields near Kerman in December, in the cold, in the brown, in the middle of nothing, the narcissus comes up white and yellow and smells so sweet it makes your eyes water. She was born in December. Tahereh named her. Tahereh said she was the one flower that blooms when everything else has given up.

That December my daughter was sixteen. She was tall, taller than her mother, and thin, and quick, and she laughed with her whole face, and she was always, always reading. She read Hafez [haa-FEZ], the great poet, who lived six hundred years ago in Shiraz [shee-RAAZ] and wrote the poems every Iranian knows by heart, even the ones who say they hate poetry. She read English books she bought secondhand in Kerman with her pocket money, slowly, with a dictionary, moving her lips. She wanted to go to university in Tehran [teh-RAAN] and study English literature and translate Hafez into English properly, she said, because every English Hafez she had found was, in her words, a stranger wearing his coat.
“How do you know,” I asked her, “if you can’t read English yet?”
“I can read enough to know when someone is wearing a coat that doesn’t fit, Baba [BAA-baa],” she said. Baba means dad. She was right, too. She usually was.
Here is the thing I have to tell you now, because if I tell it later you will think I am hiding it, and I have hidden enough.
The summer before, the summer of 2003, I built Narges a new room.

Our house was an old house, mostly khesht, with the domed rooms of my grandfather and a courtyard with a pool in the middle and an orange tree. Narges had been sleeping in a corner of the domed room with her mother and me, behind a curtain, and she was sixteen and she wanted a room of her own. Of course she did. And she did not want a dome. She had seen pictures in a magazine from Tehran: a room with a flat ceiling and smooth white walls and a window with a metal frame and a desk. A modern room. A room like people have.

I am a mud man. I told her mud keeps you cool in summer and warm in winter, and breathes, and a dome is the strongest shape God made. She rolled her eyes so far back I worried for them. Her mother took her side. So I built it.

I built it on the roof of the old kitchen, against the courtyard wall, with walls of fired brick, and on top I poured a flat roof of concrete. The concrete was the heavy part. It sat on the walls like a lid. It was not built to the code, the earthquake rules the government wrote in 1988. I will tell you about the code later. I knew the code existed. Everyone knew it existed, the way you know there is a law about speeding. I used thinner steel in the roof than the drawings say, and fewer pieces of it, because steel was expensive that year and I was paying for the room with the money we had saved for her university. I did not tie the roof to the walls with the band of steel the code asks for, because I had never seen anybody in Bam do it. I built it the way everybody built.
Narges painted the walls white herself, and put her books on a board on bricks, and hung a picture of Hafez’s tomb on the wall, and was happier than I had seen her since she was a little girl.
I am telling you this so that you know. I am not asking you to forgive me. I am only telling you, so that you know.
At night, after work, I smoked a little opium.

I will say this plainly too, because in Kerman it is not the scandal you might think. In our part of Iran, opium has been around for a very long time. It comes over the border from Afghanistan, which is not far, carried through the desert on camels and in trucks and on the backs of men, and some of it stays. Old men smoke it at the end of the day the way old men in other countries drink a whisky. It is called taryāk [tar-YAAK]. You heat a little black ball of it on the end of a long clay pipe called a vāfur [vaa-FOOR], held over a little dish of glowing charcoal, and you breathe in the smoke, and your back stops hurting, and the edges of the world go soft and warm like a blanket fresh from the line, and you can sit in your courtyard under the stars and listen to the water in the pool and not think about money.

I was not one of the men who could not stop. I told myself that. I smoked a little, three or four nights a week, after a day of treading mud. My back was the back of a man who had stamped on wet earth for thirty years. Tahereh did not like it. She did not say much. She opened the window when I came to bed.
I tell you because it matters later, and because I promised myself I would leave nothing out that made me look better than I was.
2. The Oasis Clara
The bus from Kerman took four hours, and for three and a half of them there was nothing to look at but the end of the world.

I had my face against the window. Outside, the land was the colour of a lion. Flat, then folded, then flat again, a brown-gold plain running out to mountains that were not quite real, bare blue-grey ridges standing in the haze like stage scenery painted on gauze. No trees. No houses. Every half hour a single mud building beside the road, a teahouse or the ruin of one, with a broken tower like a chimney, which I later learned was a wind-catcher, a kind of old air-conditioner that catches the breeze up high and pours it down into the rooms. Once, a line of camels walking parallel to the road, slow and indifferent, with nobody leading them. Once, far off, a whirlwind of dust, a pale column turning in the sun like a dancer, crossing the plain all by itself.

I am a conservator. I repair old buildings made of earth. In Germany that is less strange than it sounds; half the farmhouses in Bavaria have walls of clay packed into a wooden frame, and somebody has to look after them, and for nine years that somebody had been me. I am good with my hands and bad with people, which is a common combination in my profession. I can tell you, by rubbing a pinch of plaster between my fingers, roughly what century it was mixed in. I cannot tell you what to say to a man whose father has just died. I know that because, that autumn, I had been the man’s daughter, and I had not known what to say to myself either.

My father died in September, in Regensburg [RAY-genz-boorg], of the kind of cancer that gives you three months’ notice and then keeps to its word. He was a carpenter. He taught me to plane a board when I was seven and to read the grain in wood the way you read a face. When he was dying, in the hospital, he asked me one thing. He said, Clara, don’t spend Christmas at the house. Go and see something.

So I was on a bus in the southeast of Iran, four days before the longest night of the year, going to see the largest building made of earth that human beings have ever raised. My colleagues in Munich thought I was mad. My mother thought I was grieving, which was the same thing to her. I thought nothing. I had stopped thinking in September. I was only going.
And then, at the end of the fourth hour, the bus came over a low rise, and there it was.
I want to describe it properly, and I am not a writer, so I will do what I do with a wall: I will go slowly, from the outside in.

First there was a line of dark green along the bottom of the sky. It did not look like trees. It looked like a band of shadow lying on the desert, or a long low cloud that had come down to rest. As we drew closer the band grew taller and broke into separate shapes, and then the shapes became palms, thousands upon thousands of date palms, standing so close together that their crowns made a single roof, dark and glossy and moving very slightly in a wind I could not feel. Below the palms, walls. Mud walls, everywhere, the same pale gold as the desert, running in every direction, enclosing gardens, enclosing orchards, so that the whole oasis looked like a honeycomb made of earth with green poured into every cell. I saw oranges. In December, in the desert, I saw orange trees heavy with fruit, so many oranges that the trees looked lit from within, little suns hanging in the shade.
And above it all, to the right as the bus turned, on its rock, the Arg.

I had seen photographs. Everyone in my field has seen photographs. The photographs are lies. They are true about the shape, and the shape is extraordinary: the great wall with its round towers marching along the crest like the knuckles of a fist, the town inside the wall climbing the rock in a confusion of roofs and domes and lanes, and at the very top the citadel, the castle, built up in terraces, square and tall and fierce, like a thing that has been watching the desert for a thousand years and has not yet seen anything it is afraid of. But a photograph cannot tell you the colour. It is the colour of the desert, exactly. It is the desert, standing up. Somebody took the ground and raised it into towers and the ground did not mind. The Arg does not sit on the landscape the way a castle in Germany sits on its hill, like a crown put on a head. It grows out of it. You cannot see where the rock stops and the walls begin.

I was still looking at it, with my mouth open, when the bus pulled into the station in a cloud of its own dust, and a boy of about ten knocked on the window beside my face and shouted, in English, “Hotel! Hello! Mister! Hotel!”
“I’m not a mister,” I said through the glass.
He considered this, unbothered. “Hotel, missus!”

The guesthouse was in the old part of town, a few streets from the Arg, an old merchant’s house that the owner had turned into rooms for travellers. You went in through a heavy wooden door in a blank mud wall, through a dark passage that turned twice so nobody in the street could see in, and came out into a courtyard. In the middle of the courtyard there was a pool, a long rectangle of still water, and at one end an orange tree, and around all four sides the rooms opened onto a covered walk under arches. The arches were mud. The rooms were mud, with domed ceilings. The beds were thin mattresses on the floor with heavy red blankets, and the walls were so thick that my room was as quiet as the inside of a church.

There were other travellers. That December there were maybe a dozen of us. A Japanese man who was cycling from Istanbul to Delhi and had legs like a racehorse and the manners of a duke. Two Dutch girls who had been in Iran a month and dressed better than the Iranian women. A silent Englishman reading a very fat book. A young Australian couple on their honeymoon, overland to India, who held hands under the table at dinner as if the table might take one of them away. The road through Bam was the old road to Pakistan and India, and for forty years people like us had been coming down it, the hippies first and then the backpackers, and Bam was where everybody stopped to rest before the last hard stretch of desert to the border. The guesthouse’s book was full of thank-you notes in twenty languages. I read it the first night by the light of a gas lamp, under four blankets. Best dates of my life, a Canadian had written in 1996. And under it, in a different hand, a German: Best everything.

In the corner of the courtyard, beside the orange tree, there was a doorway that went down. Steps cut into the earth, steep and narrow, descending into the dark under an arch. Cold air came up out of it, smelling of wet stone.
“What is that?” I asked the owner, a gentle man with a grey beard.

“The water,” he said. “Under. Old water. Very old.” He made a gesture with his hand, a flat line moving along under the floor. “Qanat [gha-NAAT]. Tomorrow, maybe, someone explains you. Is a long story.”
I stood at the top of the steps for a while, feeling the cold breath of the earth on my face. It was the first time in three months I had been curious about anything.
3. The Worm and the Apple Ayoub

She came up to the Arg on her second morning with a notebook and a little bag of tools on her belt, and she walked straight past the ticket man and past the place where the tourists stand to take their photographs, and climbed up to where my crew was working on the wall of the old stables, and squatted down beside my mixing pit and put her hand in my mud.

My men stopped work. A woman, a foreigner, with her bare hand in Ayoub’s mud. The youngest of my crew, who was nineteen and an idiot, laughed out loud. I said nothing. I wanted to see what she would do.

She lifted a handful, squeezed it, opened her hand and looked at the shape her fingers had left. She rubbed a little between her thumb and finger, slowly, with her eyes half shut, the way my father used to test it. Then she broke off a piece of straw from the mix and held it up to the light and looked at its length. Then she said something in English to me, very fast, and then saw my face, and said it again, slowly, in a terrible Persian made out of a phrase book.
“Very — good — earth.”
It was the first time in eleven years anyone who was not a mud man had said that to me. I am not ashamed to say it went straight into my chest.

Her name was Clara. She was German. She made walls of earth, she said, in her country, for old farmhouses. I did not believe there were walls of earth in Germany. I said so. She drew me a picture in her notebook: a house with a wooden frame, black beams in a crisscross, and between the beams, she pointed and said a German word, Lehm [LAYM], and touched my mud, and nodded.
Lehm. Khesht. Mud. The same word, in the end.

We could hardly speak to each other. She had perhaps thirty words of Persian and I had perhaps forty of English, and most of mine were about football. But a mud man and a mud woman do not need many words. For two hours that morning she watched us work and we watched her watch us. She showed me how they mix in Germany, with more straw, longer, and something she called Häcksel [HECK-sel], straw chopped very fine, almost to dust. I showed her the way my father tested the mix: you make a ball, you drop it from the height of your shoulder onto a stone, and if it cracks it is too dry and if it spreads it is too wet and if it lands and keeps its shape, like a tired man sitting down, it is right. She laughed, and dropped one, and it spread like a fried egg, and my men laughed, and she laughed harder than any of them.

Then my daughter came up the path with a bag of bread and cheese for my lunch, the way she did on Thursdays when school finished early, and saw a foreign woman squatting in her father’s mud pit, and her whole face lit up as if somebody had switched on a lamp inside it.
“Hello!” she said, in English, with all the confidence in the world. “My name is Narges. Welcome to Bam. What is your country please?”

They talked for an hour. I sat on a wall and ate my bread and cheese and watched my daughter speak English with a real foreigner for the first time in her life, and I understood perhaps one word in ten, and I did not need to understand. Her hands moved. Her face moved. She went red, and then she laughed, and then she corrected herself and Clara corrected her too and they both laughed again. She was translating for me, a little, now and then, turning and saying Baba, she says the Arg is the most beautiful building she has ever seen, and Baba, she says in Germany the mud is darker, and Baba, she asks if the walls ever fall down.
“Tell her,” I said, “they fall down all the time. That’s why they need me.”

Narges told her. Clara looked at me and nodded slowly, seriously, as if I had said something wise. I had only made a joke. But it is true. The walls fall all the time. A mud wall is always falling, very slowly, a little each year with the rain and the wind, and you put a little back each year, and that is how it stays. The Arg had been falling for two thousand years. It had never once stood still.
Before she left, Narges told Clara the story of the worm. I heard it start and I put my bread down to listen, because I like the way my daughter tells it, and because it is our story here.

In the Shahnameh [shaah-naa-MEH], the Book of Kings, which our poet Ferdowsi [fer-dow-SEE] wrote a thousand years ago and which is the story of all the old kings of Iran, there is a tale about this province. There was a poor man in Kerman, Haftvād [haft-VAAD], who had seven sons and one daughter. The daughter spun cotton with the other girls of the town. One day, eating an apple, she found a little worm inside it, and instead of throwing it away she put it in her spindle case and said, as a joke, Little worm, bring me luck, and I’ll spin twice as much. And she did. That day she spun twice as much cotton as any girl. And the next day twice as much again. Her family fed the worm. The worm grew. The family grew rich. The worm grew bigger and bigger, as big as a man, as big as a cow, and they built a fortress on a rock to keep it in, and fed it rice and milk in a great trough, and soldiers came from all over to serve Haftvād and his worm, and they became more powerful than the king. In the end it took the great king Ardashir [ar-da-SHEER] himself, disguised as a merchant, to come to the fortress and kill the worm by pouring molten lead down its throat.
That is the story. People in Kerman say the name of the province comes from it: kerm [KERM] means worm. Every scholar says that is nonsense. Every scholar is probably right. We still tell it.
“What does it mean?” Clara asked, when Narges had finished, in English. I understood that much.
Narges thought for a moment. She looked at the Arg above us, its towers against the white winter sky.
“My father says,” she said, in English, slowly, choosing each word, “that it means: be careful what you feed inside your walls. Because one day it is bigger than the walls.”

I had never said that in my life. She made it up, right there, to have something good to say to the foreigner. She was always doing that, putting her own thoughts into my mouth because she thought they would sound wiser coming from an old man. I let her. I have kept that one. I say it now. It is mine now. She gave it to me.
Then she did the thing I should have expected. She invited Clara to Yalda [YAL-daa].

“Is in three days,” she said. “The twenty-first. The longest night. You come to our house. My mother cooks. You must come. Mehmān [meh-MAAN] — guest — is a gift from God. If you say no, my mother is crying.”
Clara looked at me, to see if her father agreed. I put my hand on my chest and bowed my head a little, the way we do. What else could I do? My daughter had already invited half of Germany.
“Please,” I said, in English. One of my forty words. “Please. Come.”
4. Water Under the Desert Clara

He took me to see the water on the morning of the twentieth. Narges came to translate, in her school uniform, with a long dark coat and a dark scarf, and she skipped her first class to do it, which she told me with enormous pride as if she had robbed a bank.

We drove out of town in Ayoub’s tiny white car, which made a noise like a cough with every gear, through the palm groves, along a dirt road between high mud walls, and then out past the last gardens onto the open desert. The ground rose very gently toward the mountains in the south. And across the desert, in a long straight line, running from the mountains toward the town, there was a row of holes.

That is how it looked at first. A line of craters, one every thirty or forty metres, each one a ring of piled earth around a dark hole in the middle, like a row of anthills, or the marks of a giant’s walking stick. The line ran up the slope as far as I could see, toward the hills, getting smaller and smaller until it vanished in the haze. There were other lines too, further off, a dozen of them, all converging on the green of Bam.
“Qanat,” said Ayoub, and swept his arm along the line.

And Narges explained it, in English, and her father added things in Persian and she translated, and between them, standing in the wind with the desert cold on our faces, they gave me the most beautiful thing I learned in Iran.
A qanat is a tunnel that carries water.

In the desert it hardly rains. But up in the mountains it rains a little, and snows, and the water soaks into the ground and runs downhill underground, through the gravel, under the desert floor, deep, where the sun cannot reach it. Three thousand years ago, maybe more, the people of Persia worked out how to bring that hidden water to the surface without any pump or any machine.
You go up toward the mountains and you dig a well, a very deep one, until you hit the water. That first well is the most important. It is called the mādar-chāh [maa-DAR chaah]. The mother well.

Then you go down the slope a long way, toward the place where you want the water to come out, and you start digging a tunnel back uphill toward the mother well. The tunnel is very gently sloped, so gently you could not see it with your eye. Just enough that water will run along it by itself, but not so fast that it wears the tunnel away. And every thirty or forty metres along the way you dig a shaft straight up to the surface, to take out the earth you have dug and to let air in for the men working below. Those shafts are the holes. The rings of earth are what came out of them.

When the tunnel reaches the mother well, the water starts to run. Down the tunnel. In the dark. Under the desert. Mile after mile. And where the tunnel finally comes out at the surface, at the bottom of the slope, there is a stream of cold clear water, coming out of the ground in the middle of the desert, and it never stops. Day and night. Summer and winter. For hundreds of years. And around that stream, people plant gardens, and the gardens become a town.
“Bam,” said Ayoub, and pointed at the green behind us. “Hameh az qanat [ha-MEH az gha-NAAT]. All of it, from the qanat.”

“Some qanats here are very long,” Narges said. “Ten kilometres. Twenty. There are men whose work is to go down and clean them and repair them. Very dangerous work. My great-grandfather was one. Baba’s grandfather, on his mother’s side. Muqanni. They say a muqanni puts on a white shirt when he goes down to work, because it is already his burial shroud.”
I looked at her. She shrugged.
“It’s true,” she said. “We are a dramatic people.”

On the way back toward the groves, walking along the line of craters, Ayoub talked, and Narges translated, and I filled four pages of my notebook. I have them still. I’ll give you what I wrote, because I’ve never learned anything more beautiful about how people and earth can work together.

A qanat begins with a man who can read the ground. He walks the foot of the mountains in the autumn, slowly, looking for signs: a patch of plants greener than the rest, a line of reeds where there should be none, a dark stain of damp at the bottom of a gully. Where he thinks the water is, two diggers sink a trial well, straight down, a little wider than a man, one of them swinging a short pick and the other a short spade, while two more men stand at the top turning a wooden windlass, the charkh [CHARKH], hauling up the earth in leather buckets, the dalv [DALV]. They dig down thirty metres, fifty, a hundred, sometimes more; there is a qanat in the northeast, at Gonabad [go-naa-BAAD], whose mother well is said to be three hundred metres deep, dug nearly three thousand years ago. When they reach wet earth they dig a little pocket at the bottom and wait for days. If water seeps in, more than a bucket’s worth, they have found the mother.

Then the real work starts, at the wrong end, as they had already told me: miles down the slope, digging back uphill, blind, toward the mother, so that the water will always have somewhere to run. The slope has to be exact. Too steep, and the running water eats the floor of the tunnel and brings the roof down. Too flat, and the water stands and goes bad. A good qanat drops about one metre in every thousand. The surveyor finds that slope with a level, a rope and a plumb line, over miles, across a desert, with no instrument any of my German professors would trust. And he is right.

Down in the tunnel, the diggers keep their line by light. Two oil lamps, set one behind the other on the floor, and the digger at the face looks back along them; if they line up, he is straight. The lamps do a second job, Ayoub said, and it’s the one that matters most. When the flame shrinks and goes blue and small, the air is bad, and you get out, now, without finishing your stroke. The old diggers had a rule, he said: a flame before a foot. You never step into a dark place until you have shown it a fire.

Where the earth is soft, they line the tunnel with rings of baked clay, oval hoops called kaval [ka-VAAL], fired in a kiln and lowered down the shafts one at a time and set end to end like the ribs of an animal, so that the tunnel can’t close. And the place where the tunnel finally comes out into the light has its own name: the mazhar [MAZ-har], the place of appearing.

Then comes the part I loved most. The water belongs to everybody whose family helped pay for the digging, in shares, sometimes shares set three hundred years ago. And it is divided not by amount but by time. In the villages, the man who keeps the water, the mirāb [meer-AAB], floats a little copper bowl with a tiny hole in its bottom in a basin of water. When the bowl fills and sinks, one unit of time has passed. A fenjān [fen-JAAN]. So many fenjān for this family’s garden, then the channel is blocked with a spade of mud and opened to the next garden, and so on round the whole village, day and night, the same turn every week for centuries. A water clock, made of a bowl and a hole, keeping peace among neighbours for three hundred years.

And the water doesn’t only feed the gardens. Rich families in the old towns built their cellars over the qanat, and the cold breath of the tunnel came up through the floor, and a tower on the roof, a wind-catcher, pulled the hot air out above, so that in the worst of the summer the family sat in a cellar as cool as a church while the town outside baked. In winter, before anyone had a refrigerator, they froze qanat water in shallow pools on cold desert nights and stored the ice in great domed pits of mud brick, and ate it in July.

“There’s one more thing,” Narges said, as we reached the car. She had the look she got when she was about to say something her father would disapprove of. “In some villages, the old people say a qanat can be a man or a woman. And when a man-qanat starts to run dry, it’s because he’s lonely. So the village finds him a wife. A widow, usually. They have a little wedding. She goes down to the water and bathes in it, and then she is married to the qanat, and the water comes back.” She looked at me sideways. “It’s true. Not that the water comes back. That they do it.”
Ayoub said something short in Persian, and she laughed.
“He says,” she said, “that he has met a lot of qanats and none of them would make a good husband.”
We went down.

Not into the deep shafts. Into the place where the water came out, near the edge of the groves, where the tunnel had been opened up with steps going down to it, the way the courtyard of my guesthouse had steps. Pāyāb [paa-YAAB], Narges said, the stairs to the water. Old houses had their own, so the family could go down and draw water from the qanat that ran under the house. Ayoub went first, sideways, one hand on the wall, and I followed, and Narges came behind me, complaining about her school shoes.

Twenty steps down, the light from above was a grey square. Thirty steps down, it was a white coin. Then we were at the bottom, crouching, in a low passage cut through the earth, just high enough to walk bent over. The walls were damp, packed earth, smooth, with the marks of picks on them, little curved scoops in long rows, the strokes of hands dead for centuries. And there at our feet, in a channel cut in the floor, was the water.

It was moving. It moved quickly and silently out of the dark on our left and into the dark on our right, clear as air, so clear I could only see it because of the way it bent the light of Ayoub’s torch across the pebbles at the bottom. It was cold. I put my hand in and it was so cold it hurt my bones. It had come from under the mountains. It had been running in this dark, in this exact channel, since long before there was a Germany.

Ayoub crouched beside me with the torch, and he didn’t say anything for a long time, and neither did I. The only sound was the water, a very faint chuckle in the dark, and our breathing, and somewhere far up the tunnel a drop falling from the roof, again and again, slow as a clock.
Then he said something in Persian, quietly.

“He says,” Narges whispered, “this is the mother of Bam. Above, the town is the children. Down here is the mother. Above, everyone is very busy. Down here, the mother is just going home, the way she always goes.”
I looked at Ayoub. He was looking at the water.
“He says the whole town is built on top of the mother,” Narges said. “Every house. The guesthouse where you stay. The Arg. It’s all on top. She runs under everybody. People forget.”

When we came up, blinking, into the hard white light of the desert winter, Ayoub stood at the top of the steps for a while with his hands in his pockets, looking out across the line of craters running up toward the mother well in the hills.

“Clara,” he said. He said my name like Kelaara, three syllables. He pointed at the ground. Then he said, in English, one of his forty words, slowly, carefully, so that I would understand that he meant it.
“Strong.”

Then he pointed at the town, at the new part of Bam, where the buildings were not mud but brick and concrete, flat-roofed, with satellite dishes. And he made a face, and shook his hand from side to side, the way you do when something is so-so.
Then, very seriously, he pointed at himself, and laughed.
I didn’t understand. Narges did. She rolled her eyes.
“He thinks he is very funny,” she said. “He is saying the old ways are strong and the new ways are not so strong, and also that he is old. It is a joke he makes all the time. It isn’t even good.”
5. Yalda Ayoub
Yalda [YAL-daa] is the longest night of the year.

I want to explain it properly, so that you can see the whole of it, the way my daughter saw it, because she loved Yalda more than any night in the calendar, more than New Year, more than her own birthday.

On the last night of autumn, the night before the first day of winter, the dark is longer than on any other night. In the old days, before the Prophet, before Islam came to Iran, our ancestors believed that this was the night when the darkness was strongest, and that the sun, the light, was born again at dawn and would get stronger every day after. So on that night you did not sleep. You stayed awake with your family to keep each other company in the dark, to make sure everybody got through to the morning, and in the morning you went out to greet the new sun.

We still do it. Every family in Iran, rich and poor, in the cities and in the villages, the religious and the ones who are not. On the night of Yalda you gather at the house of the oldest person in the family. You eat. You eat red things, because red is the colour of the dawn and of life: pomegranates, anār [a-NAAR], broken open so the seeds shine like rubies in a dish; and watermelon, hendevāneh [hen-de-vaa-NEH], which you have kept from the summer in a cool place all autumn just for this, so that in the coldest night of the year you eat the taste of summer. You eat nuts and dried fruit, ājil [aa-JEEL]. You eat our dates. You drink tea until midnight and then more tea. You tell stories. The old people tell about the old days, and the children pretend to be bored, and nobody goes to bed.
And at some point in the night, somebody brings out the Hafez.

That year, Yalda was at our house, because ours had the biggest room in the family, my grandfather’s room under the dome, and since my mother died it was where the family gathered. My two sisters came with their husbands and their children, and Tahereh’s brother came from Kerman with his wife, and there were twenty of us under the dome, sitting on the carpets around a long cloth spread on the floor and covered with food. And Clara.

She came at sunset, with Narges, who had gone to fetch her from the guesthouse so she would not get lost in the lanes. She was wearing a long dark coat and a scarf she had bought in Kerman, a blue one, tied badly, so that it kept slipping back off her yellow hair, and every time it slipped all my sisters’ children stared at the yellow hair in delight, and every time Narges reached over and fixed it for her. She had brought a box of German chocolates, which she gave to Tahereh with both hands and a little bow, the way she had seen Narges do with the bread, and Tahereh was so pleased that she pretended not to be and put them away in the cupboard for an occasion. Yalda was an occasion. Tahereh put them in the cupboard anyway. That is how pleased she was.

I sat Clara in the place of honour, beside Tahereh. Tahereh looked at her for a long time, very closely, the way she looks at bread to see if it’s done. Then she took Clara’s hand in both of hers, those brown hands made hard by the bread oven and the washing, and turned it over, and looked at the palm, and felt the calluses there, and the little cracks in the skin from working with lime and mud.

“Bā-ādam [baa-AA-dam],” Tahereh said to me. A real person. “She works with her hands. She’s not one of those.” What those were, she did not say. It was high praise from Tahereh. She has said that about maybe four people in my life. I was not one of them.

We ate. Oh, we ate. Tahereh had been cooking for two days. There was rice with sour cherries, and a stew of chicken and walnuts and pomegranate syrup, dark and sweet and sour all together, which we call fesenjān [fe-sen-JAAN], and bread, and yoghurt with cucumber and dried mint, and the watermelon cut in great red wedges, and the pomegranate seeds heaped in a glass bowl in the middle of the cloth so the lamplight came through them red. Clara ate like a woman who had not eaten since September. Perhaps she hadn’t. My sisters kept piling food on her plate and saying bokhor, bokhor [bo-KHOR], eat, eat, and she kept eating and saying merci [mer-SEE], which in Iran is how we say thank you, a French word that came to us somehow and stayed, and every time she said merci my sisters laughed and gave her more.

We told stories. My uncle, who is the funniest man in our family and the worst at telling jokes, told a long story about a donkey and a mullah that Narges refused to translate, and Clara laughed anyway because everyone else was laughing so hard. My nephews did a magic trick with a coin that went wrong. My eldest sister told the story of the winter of her girlhood when the snow came to Bam, real snow, the only time in her life, before I was born, and the palms stood in the white with their heads bent like old men praying, and nobody knew what to do, and our father went out and threw a snowball at the mosque.

The lamp burned. The tea came round. Outside it was cold and very dark and very still, the dark of the longest night in the year, and inside the walls of my grandfather’s room, with the dome over us and twenty people breathing and the smell of pomegranate and charcoal and tea, it was as warm as the inside of a hand.
Then, near midnight, Tahereh said, “Narges. The book.”

Narges got up and went to her room and came back with her Hafez. A small book, very old, its green cloth cover worn grey at the corners, its pages soft as a handkerchief. It had been my grandmother’s. Narges carried it everywhere. She sat down again beside Clara, and held the book in her lap with both hands, and looked at Clara.
“Now we do fāl [FAAL],” she said. “The fāl of Hafez.”
And she explained. I listened. I knew it all, of course. But I liked to hear her explain things. She explained them better than anyone.

“In Iran,” she said, “when you want to know something about your life, about the future, you don’t go to a fortune-teller. You ask Hafez. You hold the book. You close your eyes. You make a wish, or you ask a question, in your heart, silently. Not out loud. Then you say a little prayer to Hafez, a special one, everyone knows it. And then you open the book, anywhere, without looking. And the poem on that page is your answer.”
Clara was looking at the little green book as if it might bite her. “Does it work?”
Narges smiled. It was a smile I knew. She had had it since she was four.

“It works,” she said, “the way poems work. It doesn’t tell you what will happen. It tells you what you need to hear.” She held out the book. “You make a wish. Then you give it to me and I open it for you. You can’t read Persian, so I am your hands.”

Clara held the book for a long time with her eyes closed. Everyone in the room went quiet. The children stopped eating. My uncle stopped talking. Even Tahereh, who had seen a thousand fāls in her life, leaned forward. I watched the German woman’s face, with her eyes closed and the lamp on her and her scarf slipping back again, and I knew, the way you know things at Yalda, what she was asking about. You don’t have to speak anyone’s language to know that.

Then she opened her eyes and gave the book to Narges. Narges closed her own eyes and said the little prayer under her breath, the one everyone says: O Hafez of Shiraz, you who know every secret, I ask you by Shakh-e Nabat [SHAAKH-eh na-BAAT], the one you loved… And she opened the book with her thumb, anywhere, and looked down at the page.
And her face changed.

I saw it. Everyone saw it. My sisters looked at each other. Tahereh let out her breath, slowly, through her nose. Because Narges had opened the book to one of the most famous poems Hafez ever wrote. One that every Iranian knows by heart. One that people have read at the bedsides of the dying, and at the graves of the dead, and in prisons, and in wars, for six hundred years.
She read the first line out loud, in Persian, in that clear voice of hers:
Yusof-e gomgashteh bāz āyad be Kan’ān, gham makhor.
[yoo-SOF-eh gom-gash-TEH BAAZ aa-YAD beh ka-NAAN, GHAM ma-KHOR]
Kolbeh-ye ahzān shavad ruzi golestān, gham makhor.
[kol-BEH-yeh ah-ZAAN sha-VAD roo-ZEE go-les-TAAN, GHAM ma-KHOR]
Then she translated it for Clara. Slowly. Carefully. Word by word, in her schoolgirl English, with her finger moving along under the line. I will tell you what she said, because I can still hear it.

“Yusof,” she said. “Joseph. You know Joseph? In the Bible? In the Qur’an also. The boy who is lost. His brothers throw him in a well and tell his father he is dead. And his father, Jacob, cries so much that he goes blind. But Joseph is not dead. Many years later he comes back.”
Clara nodded.

“So. The first line: Lost Joseph will come back to Canaan. Do not grieve. Canaan is his home. And the second line.” She stopped. Her finger stayed on the page. “The house of sorrows will one day become a rose garden. Do not grieve.”
The room was very quiet.

“Gham makhor,” Narges said. “That’s the end of every line in the poem. Every one. Gham makhor. It means: don’t grieve. Don’t eat sorrow. In Persian we say you eat sorrow. Gham khordan [GHAM khor-DAN]. To eat sadness. And gham makhor, don’t eat it.”
She looked at Clara and said it again, slowly, so that she could learn it. “Gham — makhor.”
“Gham makhor,” said Clara. Her voice cracked on it.

“Good,” said Narges, in English, and put her hand on Clara’s hand on the book. “Very good. You have a good accent. Now you know the most important thing in Persian. That’s all you need. Everything else is just for shopping.”

And the whole room laughed, my sisters and my uncle and the children and Tahereh, and Clara laughed with them, and wiped her eyes with the back of her hand, and said merci, and my sisters gave her more watermelon.
6. The Longest Night Clara
Narges walked me home at two in the morning, through the lanes of the old town.

I should have been frightened, perhaps. A foreign woman, alone with a sixteen-year-old girl, walking through the dark alleys of a town on the edge of the desert, at two in the morning. I was not frightened. I have never in my life felt safer than I did that night. The lanes were narrow, just wide enough for a donkey cart, and on both sides the mud walls rose higher than our heads, smooth and pale in the starlight, and the only sound was our footsteps on the packed earth and, behind the walls, very faintly, here and there, the voices of other families still awake. Laughing. A radio playing old music. A child protesting. All of Bam, behind its walls, staying up together to keep each other company through the longest night.

And the sky. I have tried, since, to describe that sky to people in Germany, and I always fail, so I will fail here too, but I will try. In Bavaria the night sky is a dark blue ceiling with some stars painted on it. Over the desert at Bam it was not a ceiling. It had depth. You could feel that the stars were at different distances, some close, some unimaginably far, as if you were looking down into deep water rather than up at a roof. There were so many of them that the dark between them was crowded. The Milky Way went straight across the top of the sky like a road somebody had swept, pale and lumpy and full of dark places where clouds of dust hid the stars behind. It was so bright that our shadows went before us along the lanes, faint and blue. It was so cold that our breath stood in the air in front of our faces like small ghosts and stayed there after we’d walked through.
“In the desert,” Narges said, “on Yalda, the old people say you can see your whole life written in the stars. If you are patient. And if you know how to read.”
“Can you read it?”
“No.” She laughed. “I’m only sixteen. You need to be old. My grandmother, before she died, could read it. She said she read my whole life in them the night I was born.”
“What did it say?”
Narges was quiet for a few steps.
“She wouldn’t tell me,” she said. “She said if she told me, I’d try to change it. And then it would happen anyway, and I’d just be tired.”
At the door of the guesthouse she stopped and took something out of her coat pocket. A folded piece of paper.

“For you,” she said. “I wrote it out. The poem. The whole thing in Persian, and some of it in English, my English. Only four lines, the ones I love most. The rest is too hard, I’m still working on it. It isn’t a good translation. It’s a stranger wearing his coat. But it’s warm.” She pressed it into my hand. “So you remember. Gham makhor.”
“Gham makhor,” I said.
“Good. Very good accent. Good night, Clara. Shab bekheir [SHAB be-KHEIR].” Good night. “Tomorrow is a longer day. Every day from now is longer. That’s the whole point.”
She turned and went off down the lane, a dark shape between the pale walls, her long coat swinging, and at the corner she turned back once and waved, and I waved, and then she was gone.
I didn’t sleep. I lay under my four red blankets in my domed room as quiet as a church and held her piece of paper against my chest and thought about my father.

What I had asked Hafez, with my eyes closed, with the green book in my hands, was whether it would ever stop. The grief. That was the whole question. Not a wish. A question. Will this ever stop. I had not cried at the funeral. I had not cried in October or November. I had cried in a stranger’s house in Iran in front of twenty people because a sixteen-year-old girl told me in her careful English that the house of sorrows would one day be a rose garden, and to stop eating my grief.
I read her translation by the light of the gas lamp. Her handwriting was round and neat, a schoolgirl’s, with the English letters drawn very carefully, as if each one were a small building.
Lost Joseph will come home to Canaan. Do not grieve.
The hut of sorrows will one day be a garden of roses. Do not grieve.
If the flood of nothing comes and pulls up the root of everything that is, while Noah is the captain of your ship, do not grieve.

The third line stopped me. I read it three times. If the flood of nothing comes and pulls up the root of everything. I didn’t know, then, what it would come to mean. I didn’t know a poem six hundred years old could have a line in it written for a week that had not happened yet.
At the bottom of the page she had written, in English, in pencil, smaller:
P.S. Hafez is never wrong. But sometimes he is early.
From the Clay

You are standing on me. You have always been standing on me. Every step you have ever taken in your life you took on me, and you did not once look down to say thank you. That’s all right. I’m not offended. I’m not anything. I’m the ground.
Let me tell you what I am, here, under Bam, so you will understand the rest.

I am old. Older than the desert. Once, long before anything you would call a person, this whole land was the floor of a sea. I remember the sea. I hold it still: the shells of small creatures pressed into my stone, the salt in my clay. Then the land to the south of here, the land you call Arabia, began to push north. It is still pushing. It has been pushing for longer than there have been flowers. A finger’s width a year, every year, never resting, shoving against the land to the north the way one great ship might shove against another, slowly, forever. And where they press against each other, I fold. I crumple. I rise up into mountains like a rug pushed against a wall. All the mountains of Iran are that rug. That’s what Iran is. A crease in me.
And where I am pushed too hard, I crack.

I am cracked all through here. Long cracks, running for hundreds of miles, under the desert, under the mountains, under the towns. You call them faults, which is a good word, because you like to have something to blame. But they are not faults. They are only where I give way. They are where I let go of what I’ve been holding.

Under a fault, the two sides of me try to slide past each other. They cannot. They are locked, held by the weight above them, by friction, by the roughness of rock against rock. So they wait. And the push from the south goes on, a finger’s width a year. And the strain builds, and builds, quietly, in the dark, for a hundred years, for a thousand, like a breath held longer than any breath has ever been held. And then, one morning, the rock can’t hold it anymore. And I let go all at once.
That is all an earthquake is. A held breath, let out.
Here is what you must understand about clay. About me, when you have shaped me.

Your people learned, ten thousand years ago, that if you took me wet and pressed me into a shape and let the sun dry me, I would stand up for you. I would be a wall. I would be a house. I would keep out the wind and keep in the warmth and hold up a roof over your children while they slept. You made me into villages, then towns, then the great earth city on the rock. You made me into the towers and the domes and the long walls, and you lived inside me, and you died inside me, and when you were done you put your dead back into me, and I took them.

I never minded. That is what you must understand. A wall of clay is honest. It knows what it is. When it is old, it softens. When it rains, it lets a little of itself go. When it falls, it falls slowly, a little at a time, over years, and you see it falling, and you come and put a little more of me back. A clay wall that falls on you is a heap of soft earth. You can dig out of it with your hands. Your people have been digging their children out of clay for ten thousand years, and most of the time, the children were still breathing.

But you are not patient, your kind. In my lifetime, which is all of time, you are a quick bright flicker, a match struck in a dark room. And lately you have been in a hurry. You found that if you burn clay in a fire it becomes brick, hard as stone. You found that if you burn stone and grind it you get a powder that sets like rock when you add water. You found you could make a roof of that, flat and heavy and smooth, and lay it on top of your walls like a lid.
You did not ask me about it. You never do.

There is a story your people tell in this province, about a girl who found a worm in an apple, and fed it, and it grew and grew until it was bigger than the walls built to hold it. You think it’s a story about greed. Maybe. It is also true, in its way, about me. Worms have been eating the old earth walls of the citadel for years: termites, tiny, blind, working in the dark inside the clay, hollowing it out from within while from the outside it looked as solid as ever. And men, wanting to save the citadel, had been patching it, adding new things to old things, heavier things, in the wrong places. And the old clay had been drying out, year by year, as the water under the town grew less.
Everything was a little weaker than it looked. That’s all. That is how it always is. Nothing ever fails all at once. It only shows that it has failed, all at once.
Here is how I would say it, if I were a song. Your people sing at the brick pits when they tread me. I have heard them for ten thousand years. I have kept the tune.
Wet me and tread me and lay me in the sun, and I’ll stand as your wall till the standing is done;
I’ll keep out the wind when the winter is deep,
I’ll hold up your roof over children asleep.
But I’m not the rock and I’m not the steel,
I’m the dust of a sea that the mountains conceal; when I’m tired of standing I’ll lie where I stood, and the earth I came out of will take me for good.

On the longest night, while the girl read the poem about the lost boy coming home, I lay under your town and held my breath, as I had been holding it for longer than your people have been keeping dates.
I wasn’t waiting. I don’t wait. I don’t know what tomorrow is.
I was only full.
II. THE GROUND CLEARS ITS THROAT
7. Small Cracks Ayoub
On the twenty-third I found a crack in the wall of my daughter’s room.

It was nothing. I want to say that first, the way I said it to myself. A hairline, thinner than a hair, running from the top corner of the window frame up toward the ceiling, at a slant. The kind of crack every new building gets in its first winter, when the cold comes and the walls shrink a little and the plaster complains. I saw it because I was in her room to fix the window catch, which she had broken by slamming it, and I stood on her chair and looked at it for a while with my nose almost touching the wall.

Then I got down, and fixed the catch, and went out into the courtyard, and stood in the sun and looked up at the room from outside. It sat on top of the old kitchen like a box on a box. White, square, modern. The concrete roof a dark grey line along the top, heavy, flat, with a little iron railing Narges had asked for, so she could stand up there in the evenings and look at the Arg. From below it looked strong. It looked like a room in a magazine.

I knew what a crack meant. A mud man knows more about cracks than about anything else on earth. A crack is the wall telling you where it’s tired. It is telling you where the weight is going and where it can’t go anymore.
I told myself it was the cold. Then I went to work.

On the way, I drove past the line of craters south of the Arg, the old qanat my grandfather died in, which still ran, just. I want to tell you what was happening to the qanats, because it was happening to everything. In my grandfather’s time there were more than sixty of them under Bam, and every one had a muqanni, and every muqanni had a son learning the work. By 2003 the old men were seventy and eighty, and their sons were driving taxis in Kerman. Nobody wanted to go down. It is cold and dark and it kills you. And there was no need, people said, because now there were pumps. A man with money drilled a deep well with a machine and put a diesel pump on it and took as much water as he wanted, from below the qanats, and the water under the desert sank lower every year, and one by one the old qanats ran thinner, and some of them ran dry. I had watched it happen my whole life. Everybody had. Nobody did anything, because the pumps were feeding the new orchards, and the new orchards were feeding the town, and the old men with their lamps and their white shirts were only old men.
Let me tell you now about the code, since I said I would.

In 1978, before the revolution, an earthquake came to the town of Tabas [ta-BAS], in the desert north of here. Tabas was a town like Bam: mud, palms, a qanat, an old citadel. In the town itself the earthquake killed almost everybody. With the villages around it, fifteen thousand people. My father went there afterwards with other men from Kerman to help dig. He came back and did not speak for a week, and when he spoke he said only, They were all inside.

Ten years after Tabas, in 1988, the government wrote rules for building. A book of them, with a number instead of a name, the way governments like. Standard 2800. It said how thick the steel should be in a concrete roof, and how many pieces, and how far apart. It said every wall should have a band of concrete with steel inside it running along the top, called a tie beam, so the walls and roof are held together like the fingers of a fist and cannot fall apart from each other. It said how deep the foundation should go. It said many things. It was a good book. I have read some of it. Engineers wrote it, men who had seen Tabas.

Then, two years after the book, in 1990, an earthquake came to the north, near the Caspian Sea, to Rudbar [rood-BAAR] and Manjil [man-JEEL], green towns in the rain, and killed forty thousand people in one night. The book had been written. Hardly anybody had followed it.

You must understand how it works here, and I think how it works everywhere. The government writes the rule. The rule says a building must be checked by an engineer. The engineer is supposed to come and look. But there are not enough engineers, and they are not paid much, and a man building a room on top of his kitchen is not going to pay an engineer to come all the way from Kerman to look at it. Or the engineer signs the paper without coming, for a little money. Or the city says you need a permit, and you get the permit by knowing somebody, or you don’t get it at all and build anyway, and nobody comes, because nobody ever comes. And steel costs money and cement costs money and the people of Bam do not have money, and they want to build their daughters a room before their daughters are married and gone.

So we built. All of us. All over Bam, for thirty years, as the town grew and the old mud houses got too small and people wanted rooms like in the magazines, we built with brick and concrete, and we built badly, because we were building the way the man down the street built, and the man down the street was still alive, and his house was still standing, so it must be fine.
I am not saying this to excuse myself. I am saying it so you understand that I was not a special kind of fool. I was the ordinary kind. There were thousands of us.
That night, I smoked.

I sat in the courtyard by the pool with the little brazier of charcoal at my feet, the manqal [man-GHAL], and my long clay pipe, and I heated the black bead of taryāk on the end of it and breathed it in, slow, and held it, and let it out. The smoke went up past the orange tree into the stars. My back loosened. My thoughts loosened. The crack in the wall went soft and far away, like a word in a dream.

Narges came out in her pyjamas with a blanket round her shoulders and sat on the edge of the pool, not near the smoke, because she hated the smell. She did not say anything about it. She never said anything about it. That was worse than saying something, and she knew it, and she knew that I knew it.
“Baba,” she said. “Clara wants to see the Arg at sunrise. Before she leaves. Can I take her? On Friday? Early?”
“Friday is the twenty-sixth,” I said.
“I know when Friday is, Baba.”
“You’ll have to be up at five.”
“I’m always up at five. You’re not up at five.”

That was true. I said she could take her. I said, wear your warm coat, it’s cold before the sun. She said, I know, Baba. She kissed me on the top of my head, which she did not do much anymore now she was sixteen, and went back to her room, up the outside stairs, onto the roof of the old kitchen, and I heard her door close, and saw her light come on, and saw her shadow cross the curtain, and then the light went out.
I sat there a long time with the pipe. I could see the roof of her room against the stars. Flat. Grey. Strong.
8. Christmas in the Desert Clara
On Christmas Eve, the travellers in the guesthouse decided to have Christmas anyway.

It was the Australians’ idea. They had been on the road for three months and the young wife, whose name I never learned to say properly, missed her family with a kind of frank cheerful desperation that made it impossible to refuse her anything. The owner, the gentle man with the grey beard, thought it was wonderful. He said that Jesus, Isā [ee-SAA], was a great prophet in Islam too, born of a virgin, Maryam [mar-YAM], Mary, and that it would be an honour. He produced, from somewhere, a small dusty plastic tree with lights on it that blinked in a sequence of red, green and a yellow that stuttered. He said a Dutch traveller had left it in 1999 and he had been waiting for an occasion.

So in the courtyard on the night of the twenty-fourth, around the long pool, with the orange tree and the stars and the cold, there were a dozen of us from eight countries, and a plastic tree, and a feast the owner’s wife made of rice and lamb and dates, and someone had found a bottle of something that was certainly not legal and certainly not wine, and we sang. The Australians sang a carol about kangaroos. The Japanese cyclist sang a song from his village, beautifully, standing up very straight with his hands at his sides. The silent Englishman, to everyone’s astonishment, put down his fat book and sang Silent Night in a deep, true voice, in German, in my language, all three verses, and then sat down and picked up the book again as if nothing had happened.
I didn’t sing. I couldn’t. My father sang that song. He sang it every Christmas Eve, badly, standing at the window of our flat in Regensburg, looking out at the snow.
On Christmas morning Narges came to the guesthouse before school. She was in her uniform, the long coat, the dark scarf, and she had something wrapped in a page of newspaper.
“For you,” she said. “Merry Christmas. I looked it up. You say Merry, not Happy. Merry Christmas.”

It was a small book. A Hafez. Not old, like hers. A cheap new edition from the bookshop in Kerman, palm-sized, with a red plastic cover and gold letters. In the front, on the first page, in her round careful hand, she had written in English: For Clara, so you can do your own fāl. You will need a Persian to read it. Please come back and find one. Love, Narges. Bam, 25 December 2003.
And under that, in Persian, a line I could not read.
“What does that say?”
She smiled the smile.
“You have to come back,” she said, “and find a Persian to read it.”

I turned the little red book over in my hands. I had a gift for her, too. I had bought it in Munich for nobody in particular, months ago, before my father died, and carried it in the bottom of my bag ever since without knowing why: a small fountain pen, dark green, German, the kind my father used to write his invoices with. I gave it to her. I said, for your translations. For when you put Hafez into English properly. For when you take the stranger’s coat off him.

She held the pen in both hands like a bird. She didn’t say anything. She uncapped it and looked at the nib in the morning light, and capped it again, and put it very carefully in the inside pocket of her school coat, on the left, over her heart, and buttoned the pocket.
“I’ll write you,” she said. “When I’m in Tehran. At the university. In English. With this. And you’ll correct my mistakes.”
“There won’t be any.”
“There will be many. Hafez will be very angry with me.” She laughed and looked at her watch. “I’m late. I’m always late. Friday at half past five? At the gate of the Arg? Sunrise?”
“Friday at half past five.”
“Don’t be late, Clara. The sun is never late. It has no excuse.”
And she ran off down the lane to school with her coat flying, one hand pressed flat against the pocket over her heart, as if the pen might try to escape.
That afternoon I went up to the Arg alone and sat on the wall of the governor’s castle at the top, the highest place, and looked out.

From up there you could see everything. The old town below the rock, a maze of mud roofs and domes and lanes, the colour of the desert, with the blue tiles of a mosque dome shining in the middle of it like a jewel dropped in sand. Beyond it the new town, grey and white, concrete and brick, flat roofs crowded with satellite dishes and water tanks and laundry. Then the palm groves, a dark green sea, rolling out in every direction to the edges of the oasis, broken by the lines of mud walls. And beyond the groves, the desert, gold and endless, going out and out to the mountains on the south, which that afternoon were sharp and blue and very close in the clear cold air, their tops dusted white with the year’s first snow.

I could see the lines of the qanats now that I knew what to look for. Long dotted lines of craters running across the desert from the mountains toward the town, like stitches in a great tan cloth. The mothers, up in the hills. The children, down here. The water going home in the dark between them.

I took out my notebook and made a drawing. I am not an artist but I can draw a wall. I drew the castle, and the towers, and the old town below. Then, on the next page, I made notes, the way I do on any building I’m looking after. I noted the long vertical cracks in the castle’s outer walls. I noted the patches where new plaster had been laid over old and the colours didn’t match, and where the new plaster was harder than the old and had begun to pull away from it.
I noted the small round holes in the base of the walls, hundreds of them, where termites had got in. I noted that the clay in the lower walls was very dry, powdery, falling away under my fingernail.
At the bottom of the page I wrote, in German, a note to myself, the way I would on a job. I have it still. The notebook came through. I don’t know how.
Lovely. Old. Very tired. Should be monitored.
9. The Ground Clears Its Throat Ayoub
On the evening of the twenty-fifth, at about ten o’clock, the ground moved.

I was in the courtyard with the pipe. Tahereh was inside, watching television, a programme with a man in a suit talking about the price of rice. Narges was in her room. The night was still and cold. And then there was a sound I have heard maybe twenty times in my life, because in Kerman the ground moves now and then, and everybody knows the sound, and it is still not a sound you get used to. A low rumble that seems to come from everywhere and nowhere, from under your feet and from the sky at the same time, like a truck going by on a road that isn’t there. Then the ground jumped. Once, sharp. Then it shook, side to side, quick, for maybe three seconds. The water in the pool slopped over the edge onto the tiles. The orange tree shook and dropped two oranges with a soft double thud into the dirt. Inside, a glass fell and broke. And then it stopped.

All over the neighbourhood, doors opened. I heard them. Voices. A dog started barking and every other dog in Bam answered it. Tahereh came out in her slippers with her chador [chaa-DOR], the long cloth a woman wraps herself in, pulled round her, her hand on the doorframe. Narges came out of her door on the roof and stood at the top of the outside stairs, looking down at me.
“Baba?”
“It’s nothing. A small one. Come down for a minute.”

She came down. We all stood in the courtyard in the cold, the three of us, listening. Over the walls I could hear the neighbours doing the same, standing in their courtyards, talking in low voices, laughing a little, the way you laugh after you’ve been frightened by nothing.

Ten minutes later, it came again. Harder. A real jolt this time, and a longer shake, five seconds, six, and over the wall somewhere a section of old mud wall came down with a soft heavy whump and a cloud of dust that went up white in the starlight, and a woman screamed, and then laughed, because nobody was under it.
I want to tell you exactly what we did next, because it is the thing I go over and over, lying awake. I have gone over it so many times the edges are worn smooth, like a stone in a pocket.
Tahereh said, “We sleep outside.”

She said it the way she says the things she has already decided, as a fact, not a suggestion. She had been a girl when the earthquakes of 1981 came, near here, two of them, a few weeks apart, that killed thousands in the villages around Golbaf [gol-BAAF]. She remembered. She said, when the ground clears its throat like that, it’s going to say something. We sleep in the courtyard. Bring the blankets.

And we did. For an hour.
