We brought out mattresses and blankets and laid them on the tiles beside the pool, and Tahereh made tea on the gas ring, and we sat out there under the stars, all three of us, wrapped up, with our breath smoking, like we were at Yalda again. Over the walls I could hear that half the neighbourhood was doing the same. Somebody had a radio on. Somebody’s baby was crying.

And it was so cold. December nights in Bam are cold, colder than people think a desert is. Near freezing. By midnight the cold had come up through the mattresses into our bones. Narges’s teeth were going. Tahereh had her blanket pulled up to her eyes. Nothing had happened since the second shake. Over the walls the voices were getting fewer. Doors were closing. People were going back inside.
I made the decision. I want to be clear about that. Nobody else made it. I was the man of the house, and I said, It’s over. It was just two little ones. Let’s go in before we all catch our death.
Tahereh looked at me. She didn’t say anything.
We went in. Tahereh and I to the old room with the dome, the room my grandfather built. And Narges, up the outside stairs, to her new room on the roof.
At the top of the stairs she turned back and called down, quietly, so as not to wake the neighbours.
“Baba. Should I sleep down there? With you?”
And I said — I said it — I said, “No, azizam [a-zee-ZAM], my dear. Your room is the strongest room in the house. It’s concrete. It’s new. Go to sleep. You’ve got to be up at five for the German.”
She went in. Her door closed. Her light came on, and went off.
10. The Third Time Clara

The first shake woke me. I had gone to bed early. I came up out of sleep to the sound of the plastic Christmas tree falling over in the courtyard with a crash, and a low roaring, and my room moving, very slightly, side to side, like a boat at a mooring. Then it stopped.
I lay there with my heart going. I had never felt an earthquake. In Bavaria the ground does not move. It is one of the things Bavarians are proudest of, though they would never say so.

I got up and went out into the courtyard in my coat. Some of the others were already there, in sleeping bags and blankets, looking up at the walls. The owner was there, calm, smiling, picking up the Christmas tree. He said it was nothing. He said this happens. Kerman, he said, and shrugged, and made a little wobbling motion with his flat hand, always little bit dancing.

The second shake came while we were all standing there. It was stronger. I felt it come up through the soles of my feet, a jolt and then a shudder, and the water in the long pool rose up in a little wave and slapped against the far end, and the orange tree shook, and from somewhere outside, in the lanes, came a soft collapsing sound and a woman’s scream and then her laugh. One of the Dutch girls grabbed my arm. The Japanese cyclist, very calmly, went and stood in the middle of the courtyard, away from the walls, and looked up at the sky. I understood that he came from a country where the ground moves often, and that he was doing what he had been taught to do. I went and stood beside him. So did the Dutch girls.
“Is that the big one?” asked the young Australian husband.
“No,” said the owner, still smiling. “Is little. Is finish now.”

We stood out there for half an hour. Nothing else happened. It got colder and colder. The Dutch girls went in first. Then the Australians. The cyclist stayed longest, standing in the middle of the courtyard with his hands in his pockets, looking at the stars, and then he too nodded to me, very politely, and said “Good night,” and went in.

I went in too. I am a sensible woman. It was below freezing. The man who owned the house had lived there all his life and said it was over. My room had walls a metre thick and a dome over it, a shape that had stood for hundreds of years. I lay down in my clothes under my four red blankets, and I set my alarm for five, because I was meeting Narges at the gate of the Arg at half past, and the sun is never late, and has no excuse.
The third shake came at about ten to five.

I was already awake. I had been awake for a few minutes, lying in the dark, waiting for the alarm, the way you do when you have to get up early and your body knows it before the clock does. And the room moved. Not much. Less than the second one. A small, quick shiver, as if the whole house had shrugged. A little dust sifted down from the dome onto my face, very fine, like flour from a sieve. I heard it whisper on the blanket.
I lay there. I thought, There. A third one. That’s three. I thought it the way you think about a bus, that it’s late.

Then the alarm went off on my wrist. I turned it off. I sat up. I put on my boots in the dark. I put on my coat. In the inside pocket of the coat, over my heart, I put the little red Hafez Narges had given me, and her folded page of the poem. I was going to ask her, at sunrise, on the wall of the castle, what the Persian line on the first page said.

I remember sitting on the edge of the mattress with my boots on, in the dark, tying the laces. I remember thinking I would go quietly across the courtyard so as not to wake the others. I remember it was very cold, and very still, and I could hear nothing, nothing at all, not a dog, not a cart, not a breath of wind. The longest night was over, and it was the stillest morning I had ever known, and the town was asleep, and in half an hour the sky would start going grey over the mountains, and I would climb up the rock to watch the sun come back to Bam with a girl who believed that every day from now on would be longer.
I stood up. I looked at my watch. It said twenty-five past five.
I took one step toward the door.
From the Qanat
Let me tell you about the water, since you have met it. Since the girl’s father took the German woman down the steps to touch it.

I hold it. That is my whole relationship to water: I hold it, and I let it go. Up in the mountains to the south of this town, the snow melts in the spring and sinks into me, down through the cracks, down into the gravel that the mountains have been shedding for millions of years, and it moves through me downhill, slowly, in the dark, a few metres a day, under the desert. It has been doing this since before there was a desert. I am full of it, down there. An underground river nobody can see, running beneath the hottest place on earth.

Your people found it. Three thousand years ago, maybe more, in this land. They found that if they dug down into me at the foot of the mountains, there was water, and that if they dug a tunnel back to it from lower down, very gently sloping, the water would come to them on its own. No pump. No wheel. No animal walking in circles.
Only gravity, and patience, and a slope so slight a marble would hardly roll on it.

I want you to understand what that took. Men went down into me with a pick and a lamp and a leather bucket, in the dark, in tunnels barely wide enough for their shoulders, and they dug. For miles. Toward a well they could not see, guided only by a rope and a lamp and the instincts of their fathers. Some tunnels took fifty years to dig. A man would start one as a boy and die before the water ran. His son would finish it. Sometimes I collapsed on them. Sometimes the water came too fast and drowned them. You have heard: they put on white for the work, already dressed for burial. They knew me. They knew I give and I take and I do not explain.

And yet they kept digging. Across this whole land, from here to the borders of China, to the mountains of Afghanistan, to the deserts of Arabia and Africa, your people dug these tunnels into me, until there were tens of thousands of them, enough tunnel, if you laid it end to end, to wrap around the whole world many times. Every green place in the desert of Persia for three thousand years was a gift that I gave and that men carried up out of the dark on their backs. That is the oldest bargain between your kind and mine, here. It was a good bargain. It was honest.
Lately the bargain has been changing. I want you to see this.

You stopped digging qanats. They were too slow. You found you could drill straight down into me with a machine, deep, much deeper than any qanat, and pump the water up with a motor and diesel, as much as you wanted, whenever you wanted. A qanat only gives what the mountain gives; it takes no more than comes in. A pump takes whatever you ask. You asked for a great deal. More gardens, more orchards, more people. And the water under the desert went down. And down. The old qanats, dug at the old level, began to dry up, one by one, because their mother wells were now standing above an empty floor. And the clay above them, the clay of the town and of the old earth walls, which had always had a little moisture in it from below, began to dry too. Clay that has dried out is brittle. It cracks. It lets go.

Nothing I am telling you made the earth shake. I want to be fair. The shaking was mine, and it would have come no matter what you did. But everything I am telling you made what was standing on me weaker than it looked when the shaking came. Pump. Concrete. Termites. Patches. Thin steel. A room built for a daughter on the roof of an old kitchen. A hundred small things, all leaning the same way, quietly, for years.
You always want there to be one thing. There is almost never one thing.
Your diggers had a song for it. I’ll give it to you the way I heard it, through a hundred metres of rock, sung low in the dark to keep the fear off:
Under the sand where the diggers went down in shirts that were white as the shroud of the town, the mother runs cold in the dark, going home, and gives what the mountain gives, never a loan.
Where the water comes up, there the rock has been split; where the gardens are green, there’s a crack under it.
So drink from my hand, drink the sweet and the cold: the gift and the grave are the same, and are old.

On the evening of Christmas, under the town, the water was moving in the qanats in the dark as it always moved, going home. And at the edge of the town, along a crack that ran north and south right under the houses, a crack your scientists had drawn on their maps a little way to the east but had not seen running here, under the town itself, the rock trembled. Twice. And then, just before dawn, a third time. Small things. Throat-clearings.

Some of your people heard them and came out under the stars. Some of them went back to bed because it was cold, and because the man of the house said it was over, and because the people who had always lived here had been through a hundred little shakes before and nothing came of them.

I don’t blame them. I’m telling you so you will understand. Your people have always lived on top of me, here, in the crease where two great lands are pressing together, because this is where the water is. The water comes out where I am cracked. The springs, the qanats, the oases, they follow the faults, the way roads follow rivers. The very thing that made Bam possible is the thing that was about to undo it. The water and the crack are the same gift.
That is the oldest thing I know. The place where I give you life is always the place where I can take it.
III. FIVE TWENTY-SIX
11. Five Twenty-Six Ayoub

I will tell you this slowly. I have only ever told it fast, in pieces, to men from the government with clipboards, and to a doctor, and once to my wife, when we were both drunk on grief and could not stop. I have never told it slowly. Slowly is the only way to tell it true.

I was asleep. Tahereh was asleep beside me. In the old room, under the dome my grandfather built. Across the courtyard was the big room, the room my father extended with fired brick and a flat wooden ceiling in 1975, when I was a young man still living under my father’s roof; nobody slept in it now. Narges was up. I know she was up because her light was on. I had woken for a moment at about five, the way you wake when you hear your child moving in the house, and through the gap in our curtain I saw the square of yellow from her window on the roof. I thought: she’s getting ready for the German. I thought: wear your warm coat. I did not say it. I went back to sleep.
What woke me the second time was not a sound. It was being lifted.

You have to understand that an earthquake is not what you think. You think of shaking, side to side, a house rocking like a boat. That is what the little ones are. That is what the two the night before had been. This was not that.
The ground came up.

All of it, at once, straight up from underneath, like a fist punching the floor of the world from below. I was thrown up off the mattress. Not far, a hand’s width, maybe two, but up, into the air, and I came down hard on my back, and before I could understand anything it hit again, and again, from underneath, and the room was not a room anymore, it was the inside of a drum that a giant was beating with both fists. And the noise. People who were not there always ask about the noise. I can’t tell you. It was every noise. It was a roar so deep you didn’t hear it with your ears, you heard it with your ribs, with your teeth, a roar coming up out of the ground as if the earth itself were screaming, and on top of it the sound of everything breaking. Walls cracking, a sound like gunshots, one after another, very close. Glass. Brick. Wood. The ceiling. A long tearing, grinding noise that I later understood was the whole town coming down at the same moment, every house in Bam, tens of thousands of them, falling together, and the sound of all of that falling coming in from every direction like the sea.
It lasted, they say, about twelve seconds.

I have counted to twelve many times since. Slowly. One. Two. Three. It is not a long time. You can boil no water in it. You can say a short prayer. You can tie one shoe. You can say Narges, the way I said it, shouting it, into the dark, eleven or twelve times.
Then it stopped.
Then it was dark, and I couldn’t breathe.

The dust. Nobody who wasn’t there understands the dust. When a city of clay falls, the clay goes into the air. All of it. In a second the air was solid, thick as flour, hot from the friction, and it went into your mouth and your nose and your eyes and down your throat and you choked, and coughed, and choked, and every cough pulled more of it into you. I was on my face on the floor with plaster and broken khesht across my legs. I couldn’t see anything. Not dark like night. Dark like being inside the earth. I could hear Tahereh coughing beside me. I could hear, from everywhere, outside, a sound beginning. A thin, high sound, rising. It was people. The whole of Bam waking up under its own houses and beginning to scream.

I got my legs out. It was only the skin of the dome, the plaster and a few bricks that had come away from the inside of it, and a cut along my shin that I did not feel until the afternoon. I dragged myself out. I found Tahereh by her coughing and by her hands, which were reaching for me in the dark. Her face was wet. Blood or tears, I don’t know. She was saying my name over and over in a voice like a crow. I pulled her toward where I thought the door was, and it was there, but half of it was filled with fallen plaster, and I crawled through the gap that was left on my hands and knees, pulling her, and came out into the courtyard into the cold.

The cold was the first thing. The cold and the stars. The dust was settling, a little, already, and through it, above me, there were the stars, the same stars as Yalda, white and sharp and enormous, looking down on Bam exactly as they had looked down on it for a thousand years, as if nothing at all had happened.
And the second thing was the silence of the courtyard. The water in the pool was gone. The pool had cracked and emptied. The orange tree was standing.

The third thing was the dome. I turned on my knees and looked back at the room we had crawled out of. My grandfather’s dome, made of khesht, a hundred years old. Cracked, shifted, dust pouring out of the doorway like smoke from a chimney, but standing. It had held. It had held over Tahereh and me the way it had held over my grandfather, and my father, and me when I was a boy, and I knelt in the courtyard and looked at it and did not yet understand what that meant.
I turned around to look at the roof of the old kitchen.
There was no roof of the old kitchen.
There was no room on it.

Where my daughter’s room had been there was a shape against the stars that I didn’t understand. Flat. Too low. A great grey slab, tilted, with one corner up and the other corners down, lying on a heap of broken brick. The concrete roof. It was in one piece. It had not broken. It was the only thing in the courtyard that had not broken. It had simply come straight down, the whole heavy flat lid of it, through the room, through the walls, which had burst out sideways and spilled into the courtyard like a split sack of grain, through the old kitchen underneath, all the way down to the ground, and it was lying there, in one piece, on top of everything that had been under it.
The little iron railing she had asked for was still on top of it, bent, standing up against the stars like the frame of a broken kite.

I don’t remember crossing the courtyard. I remember being on the slab. I remember lying on it with my face against the cold concrete, the concrete I had poured with my own hands in July, and shouting her name into it, and putting my ear to it, and listening. I remember Tahereh beside me, also lying on it, also listening. I remember that we were both whispering shhh, shhh, to each other, to the town, to the screaming coming from every direction, shhh, so that we could hear her.
We couldn’t hear anything. There was a hand’s width between the slab and the bricks under it, at the edge, and I put my arm in up to the shoulder and felt only broken brick and dust and the cold.

It was twenty-five past five, maybe twenty-seven, when it happened. They say twenty-six minutes and fifty-two seconds past five. Scientists have measured it. I didn’t know the time. I only know that when I started digging it was dark, and when the sky started going grey over the mountains I was still digging, and when the sun came up, a little before half past six, red and enormous through the dust, the way it always comes up over Bam, I was still digging, with my hands.

We had nothing. No tools. The spade was under the kitchen. Our neighbour came over the broken wall from his house, which had also fallen, with a pickaxe, because his wife and his two sons were alive and he wanted to help somebody. He and I tried to lift the edge of the slab with the pick. It did not move. It was a whole roof, five metres by four, of concrete and steel. It weighed more than a truck. So we dug under it from the side, at the edge where the wall had burst out, where I knew the head of her bed had been, against the window. We dug with our hands and the pick and a broken piece of door. We pulled out bricks one at a time and threw them behind us. Tahereh pulled them away from behind us, and as she pulled them she said the prayers for the dying, out loud, steadily, one after another, between one brick and the next, the whole time, and I wanted to scream at her to stop and I couldn’t scream at her because I couldn’t spare the breath.
At a little after eight we found her shoe. Her school shoe, the black one, the one she complained about.
It was on her foot.
I will tell you the next part and then I will stop for a while.

She was lying on her side, on the floor of her room, between the bed and the door. Not in the bed. She had got up. She was dressed. She had her long dark school coat on, buttoned, and her scarf, and her shoes. She had been ready. She had been on her way to the door, to come down the stairs and go and meet the German woman at the Arg to watch the sun come up. She was one step from the door. One step. A little more than a metre.

The slab had come down at an angle, one side lower than the other. The low side was the side with the bed. The door side was higher. There was a space, a little space, by the door, between the slab and the floor. If she had taken one more step, she would have been in that space.
I don’t know that. I’m a mud man, not a scientist. I’m only telling you what I saw, and what I have thought about every day since, which is that the room I built her was a metre too short.

She was very peaceful. I want to say that. Her face was not hurt. There was dust in her eyelashes and on her lips, pale dust, the colour of Bam, as if she had fallen asleep in a field. The doctor said later it would have been very fast. That’s what they say. I’ve decided to believe it.

I wiped the dust from her eyelashes with my thumb. I did it slowly, one eye and then the other, the way her mother used to wipe sleep from them when she was small and would not wake for school. The dust would not all come. It was in the lashes, fine as flour, and every time I wiped, a little more stayed. I stopped. I thought: let her keep some. It is the earth of her own town. She was born on it and she learned to walk on it and she was going to walk on it this morning to the Arg, to show a stranger the sun. Let her keep a little of it. I took my hand away and knelt there, and the sun climbed through the dust over the mountains, and she went on lying very still, as if she were listening for my step on the stairs.
Her right hand was over her heart. Pressed flat against her coat, on the left side, over the inside pocket. The way she held it when she ran.
The pocket was buttoned. I unbuttoned it. There was a fountain pen in it. Dark green. Not hers. I had never seen it before.
12. Under Clara
I took one step toward the door and the floor came up and hit me in the face.

That is what it was like. Not a shaking. A blow. As if the whole floor of the room had been struck from underneath with something enormous, a hammer the size of a house, and leapt up at me, and I went down onto it, and it leapt again, and the dome over my head made a sound I have never heard any building make, a deep groan, a sound like an animal in pain, and then a crack like a rifle shot, and then the world fell on me.

I don’t know how long I was unconscious. Not long, I think. When I came back I was lying on my stomach, with my face turned to one side, and I couldn’t move, and I couldn’t see, and I couldn’t breathe.

The dust. You’ve heard about the dust. I had been in plenty of old buildings in my life when walls came down during restoration, and I knew clay dust, and this was not that. This was the air turned into earth. I was breathing earth. I put my face into the crook of my arm and breathed through the sleeve of my coat, short, shallow breaths, through the wool, and coughed, and breathed, and coughed, and slowly, very slowly, the dust began to settle, and I could breathe a little.
Then I tried to move, and couldn’t.
I want to describe where I was precisely, because precise is the only thing I had left down there and I held on to it like a railing.

I was lying face down on the floor, in the passage just outside my room, with my head toward the courtyard and my feet toward the room. I had taken one step through the doorway, and the floor had thrown me forward, through it, into the little arched passage that led out under the colonnade. The door frame of my room was behind my knees. My legs were in the doorway. Something heavy was across them, below the knee, pinning them to the floor. I couldn’t see it. I could feel it: rough, uneven, massive, warm. Fallen dome. Clay and brick. It didn’t hurt, at first. It didn’t hurt for a long time. That frightened me more than pain would have.

Above me, about a hand’s width above the back of my head, there was something solid. I reached up in the dark and felt it. A curve. Brick, under a skin of plaster, cracked across, bending over me from one side to the other. The arch. The little pointed arch of the passage, which had held. Above it I could hear things still moving, settling, small trickles of earth and the occasional clunk of a brick shifting, and I knew that the whole weight of the fallen room was lying on that little arch, and the arch was holding it up off me, and that it is the nature of an arch to turn weight into strength, to take what presses down on it and push it sideways into the walls, and that this is why people have been building them for five thousand years. I lay under it and thought, with a completely clear and professional part of my mind: pointed arch, mud brick, gypsum mortar, probably seventeenth or eighteenth century, very good work.
And then, because I was German and I was a conservator and I was lying under a fallen building, I laughed. In the dark. Into my sleeve. It was not a good laugh. But it was a laugh.

On my left, there was a wall. The wall of the passage. On my right, toward the courtyard, there was nothing. A gap. Dark. And from that gap, very faintly, so faintly I almost didn’t notice it, there came a breath of air.
Cold air. Clean. Damp. Smelling of wet stone.

I knew that smell. I had smelled it on my first evening in Bam, at the top of the steps in the corner of the courtyard, by the orange tree, and again six days ago at the bottom of the steps in the desert, crouched beside Ayoub and Narges, with my hand in the running water.

The pāyāb. The stairs down to the qanat. The way down to the old water that ran under the town. The steps had been just past the end of this passage, at the corner of the courtyard. The courtyard was gone, I supposed, buried. But the steps went down into the ground, and the ground had not fallen, because the ground cannot fall, and the steps were cut into it, and somewhere down there, in the dark, the water was still running, and the air of the tunnel, which had been breathing in and out of that stairway for three hundred years, was still breathing, and some of its breath was finding its way up through the rubble to me.
I put my face toward it. I breathed it. It was the most beautiful thing I have ever breathed.

It was cold. I’ll say that now and not keep saying it, because it was cold the whole time and if I tell you every time you will stop hearing it. It was below freezing that first morning. I was lying on a stone floor in a winter coat, with my legs pinned, with no blanket, and the cold came up through the floor into my belly and my chest and settled there and never left.

The cold saved me. I know that now. A doctor in Kerman told me afterwards. If it had been summer, I would have been dead of thirst in a day and a half. In the cold, your body doesn’t sweat, and you lose water slowly. The cold made me suffer, and the cold kept me alive. I’ve thought about that a great deal since. About how the same thing does both.
I could hear the town.

At first only the screaming, everywhere, near and far, rising and falling like weather. I won’t describe it. Then, under it, as the minutes went by, other sounds. People calling names. Men’s voices shouting to each other, giving instructions. Someone, very close, on the other side of the courtyard, crying in a steady exhausted rhythm, like a machine. A dog. A car horn going on and on, stuck. And somewhere above me, over the rubble, the sound I wanted most: digging. Scraping. The clink and thud of bricks being lifted and thrown aside.

I shouted. I shouted Hilfe [HIL-feh], which is help in German, and help, and komak [ko-MAK], which is help in Persian, one of my thirty words. I shouted until my throat was raw. The dust had got into it and my voice came out as a croak, a thin, cracked thing that went nowhere. I hit the wall beside me with my fist. I hit the floor. I knocked on the arch above my head. Three knocks. Three knocks. Three knocks. The way you’re supposed to, the way everyone knows.

The digging went on, somewhere above and to the right. Voices. I heard the owner, the gentle man with the grey beard, I was sure it was him, shouting a name I didn’t know, a woman’s name, over and over. His wife’s name, I think. I heard one of the Dutch girls crying, and then I heard her being pulled out, I heard the men shout and the bricks go and her scream of pain and then the men’s voices go away, carrying her. I heard someone call, in English, with an Australian accent, Sarah! Sarah! and nobody answer, and then, after a long time, the man’s voice making a sound I won’t describe.
I shouted. I knocked. Three knocks. Three knocks.
Nobody came.

I understood, later, why. The whole house had fallen. Every room. There were people under all of it, and the people digging were the people who had happened to be standing near the doors, or who had been in the strongest rooms, and they had their hands and nothing else, and they dug where they heard voices, and they dug where they knew someone had been sleeping, and they dug toward the people they loved first. They dug my room, I think. I heard them, once, behind me, beyond my feet, digging and calling and lifting. They dug into my room, where my mattress had been, and found it empty, and went away. They didn’t know I’d taken a step. Nobody knew I’d taken a step. I hadn’t known it myself until I was lying in the passage with my legs in the doorway.

The light came at some point. Not much. A grey stain somewhere off to my right, beyond the gap where the air came in, so faint I could only see it if I didn’t look straight at it. Day. Then, after what might have been hours, it got a little brighter. Then, after more hours, it went away again.
By then I had stopped shouting. My voice was gone. I knocked, every so often, three knocks on the arch with the knuckle of my right hand, until the knuckle bled, and then with the flat of my palm.

My legs had started to hurt. It began as a deep ache and then turned into something I don’t have a word for, a heavy, hot, swollen pain, and then, later that day, it began to go away, and that was worse, because I knew what it meant when a trapped leg stops hurting.

I was thirsty. I want to tell you about thirst, and I can’t, any more than I can tell you about the sky over Bam. I had not drunk anything since a glass of tea the evening before. My mouth was full of dust and the dust had turned to mud on my tongue and dried there. I had no water. I had nothing. I had my coat and my boots and my watch and, in the inside pocket of my coat, over my heart, a little red book, and a folded page with a poem on it.
13. The Whole City Ayoub

We wrapped her in the blanket from her bed, the one with the pattern of birds that her aunt had given her, and we laid her on the door of the old kitchen, which was lying in the courtyard in one piece, and our neighbour and I carried her out through the gap where our front wall had been, into the lane.
And then I saw Bam.

I had been digging for three hours with my face in the bricks. I had not looked up. I had not seen anything but my daughter’s room. Now I stood in the lane with one end of the door in my hands and my daughter on it, and I looked up the lane toward the Arg, and I could see the Arg, from our lane, which I had never been able to do in my whole life, because there had always been houses in the way.
There were no houses in the way.
I’m going to try to tell you what it looked like. I’ve tried many times. I’ve never managed it. People hear the number, and the number is too big to see.

The lane was not a lane. It was a shallow valley of rubble, mud brick and fired brick and broken beams and dust, lying in heaps and slopes, with here and there a doorframe standing up out of it with nothing on either side, or a single wall with a window in it and sky behind the window. As far as I could see, up the lane and down, and over the tops of where the walls had been, into the next lanes and the next, it was the same. Low. Flat. A sea of broken earth, the colour of Bam, the colour of a camel, gently rolling, all the way to the palms.

The palms were standing. I want you to see that. Every palm tree in Bam was standing. Not one had fallen. They stood up out of the rubble all over the town, tall and straight, with their crowns moving very slightly in the morning air, as if nothing had happened. A palm bends. It is made to bend. It has no bones to break. Thousands of them, standing in the dust in the cold morning sun over a town that was gone.

And everywhere, on top of the rubble, there were people. Digging. Thousands of them. Men and women in their nightclothes, in blankets, barefoot, grey with dust from head to foot so that they looked like statues made of the same earth as everything else, kneeling on the heaps of their houses and pulling at the bricks with their hands. Some of them were shouting names. Some of them weren’t making any sound at all. Some of them were sitting on the rubble not digging, holding someone across their knees. There were bodies in the lane, already, laid in a row along the edge where people had carried them out, wrapped in blankets and carpets and curtains and sheets, with their feet sticking out at the end, bare feet and slippers and shoes. I counted eleven in our lane before I stopped counting. Children’s feet among them.

And no help. That is the thing that people who weren’t there don’t understand. Nobody came. Not that morning. There was no one to come. The police station had fallen with the policemen in it. The fire station had fallen with the trucks inside. The hospitals had fallen with the doctors and the nurses and the patients inside. The Red Crescent office, the town hall, the governor’s office, the telephone exchange, the army barracks, everything. All the people in Bam whose job it was to help, to come, to dig, to save, were under their own houses or under their offices, or were digging out their own families with their own hands like everybody else. The whole town had been knocked down at once, and the whole town was its own rescue team, with nothing but its fingernails.

The telephones were dead. The electricity was dead. The water, the town water from the pipes, was dead. Nobody outside knew. I learned later that it was hours before anybody in Kerman understood what had happened. Someone drove out of Bam in a car at seven in the morning and got to the next town and found a telephone. That’s how the world found out about Bam. One man in a car.
I looked up at the Arg.

Every morning of my life I had seen it on its rock, with its walls and its towers and its castle at the top, the governor’s castle, square and tall against the sky. That morning, in the cold red sun through the dust, it was a hill.

That’s all. A hill. The great outer wall was broken in a dozen places, the towers slumped and split like loaves of bread pulled apart by hand. The town inside the walls was gone, every house, every lane, every dome, melted down into heaps. And the castle at the top, the high citadel, the thing I had looked at every morning and every evening for fifty-two years, the thing that turned gold and orange and red and violet every sunset, the castle was a cone of earth. A heap, with some broken walls sticking out of it. The square tower was gone. The top of the rock was the shape the rock had been before anybody built anything on it.
Two thousand years. Twelve seconds.

I’d made bricks for it for eleven years. I’d laid them into the walls with my own hands. And I stood in the lane holding one end of a door with my daughter on it, and I looked at the hill where the Arg had been, and I didn’t feel anything at all about it. Not then. It was as if somebody had told me about a building in another country. I had no room in me. All the room was on the door.

We carried her to the end of the lane, to where the lane met the main road, where people were bringing the bodies to lie them in rows, because someone had said trucks would come. We laid her down. Tahereh sat down beside her on the ground, and put her hand under the blanket and found our daughter’s hand, and sat with her, in the dust and the cold, and didn’t speak.
And I went to look for the German woman.

I don’t know why. I’ve asked myself. Maybe because I couldn’t sit there. Maybe because Narges had been going to meet her, and that was the last thing Narges had wanted to do, and somebody should do it for her. Maybe because she was a stranger, and a guest, and a guest is a gift from God, and you don’t leave a gift from God under a house. I don’t know. I went.

The guesthouse was four lanes over, toward the Arg. It took me an hour to get there, climbing over the rubble where the lanes had been, because there were no lanes anymore and I didn’t know which heap was which, and I kept stopping, because people kept calling to me for help, and I helped. A man and his son lifting a beam off a woman. An old man who couldn’t find his wife’s room in the heap of his house and kept asking me where the kitchen was, and I didn’t know, and I helped him dig where he thought, and we found a cupboard, and he sat down and cried.

When I found the guesthouse, it was a heap like all the others. The long wall along the lane had fallen outward. The courtyard was a pit of rubble. I could see the top of the orange tree, standing up in the middle of it, just like ours, with oranges still on it. The owner was there, the man with the grey beard, digging on one side of the courtyard with three other men, and there were travellers sitting in the lane, three or four of them, grey and bloody, wrapped in blankets, one of the yellow-haired Dutch girls with her leg tied up in a scarf, the Japanese man with the legs of a horse sitting very straight with his eyes closed and his arm in a sling made of a towel, and the Australian husband, alone, on a step, not moving, not looking at anything.
I asked the owner about the German woman. He looked at me for a long moment with his face grey with dust and a long cut across his forehead.

“Her room is empty,” he said. “We dug it. First thing. Her room is there.” He pointed to the corner of the heap, by where the orange tree was. “We dug to her bed. Her bed was empty. Her bag was there, her things. But not her.”
“Then where?”

He shook his head slowly. “She went to the Arg,” he said. “She told me. Yesterday. She said, tomorrow I go to the Arg very early, half past five, to see the sun. With a girl. I said, it’s still dark then. She said, I know. She left before. Before it.” He looked up the hill toward where the Arg had been. “She was up there. Waiting for the girl.”
I stood in the lane outside the fallen guesthouse and looked up at the heap where the castle had been, the cone of earth at the top of the rock.

And I saw it. You understand? I saw it the way you see a thing in a dream, all at once, whole. The German woman, alone, in the dark, on the wall of the castle, the highest place, with her coat buttoned up, waiting. Looking down at the town for a tall thin girl in a long coat coming up the path. Looking at her watch. And the girl not coming. The girl one step from her own door. And then the ground coming up, and the castle coming down, and the stranger and the hill going together into the dust.
My daughter had invited her. My daughter had told her the sun is never late. My daughter had sent her up there.

I didn’t say anything to the owner. I turned around and climbed back over the rubble the way I had come, to the end of our lane, where my wife was sitting in the dust beside a blanket with birds on it.
I sat down on the other side of the blanket. I didn’t tell her. I don’t think I said anything to anybody for the rest of that day.
14. The First Night Clara
The second time the dark came, it stayed.

I could tell the night from the day only by the cold. In the day the cold was bad. At night it was something else. It came up out of the floor and down out of the rubble and in from the gap on my right with the breath of the qanat, which was damp and colder than the air, and it wrapped around me and went into me like water into a sponge. I shook. I shook so hard my teeth knocked, and then I made my jaw tight to stop them, and then I shook in my chest instead, in great slow shudders, like sobbing without tears. I couldn’t cry. I had no water to cry with.

The ground moved, many times. Aftershocks. Some small, a shiver, a trickle of earth somewhere over my head. Some big. Once, in the night, a big one, a real jolt, and the rubble above me groaned and shifted and settled, and something came down onto the arch above my head with a heavy thud and a fall of dust on my neck, and I lay there with my eyes shut tight and my hands over my head waiting for it to come through. It didn’t. The arch held. Good work. Seventeenth or eighteenth century. I said it out loud, or I thought I did. My voice was a scraping in the dark.
I talked to my father.

Not out loud. In my head. He was there more than he had been since September. I told him where I was. I described the arch, the gypsum mortar, the way the bricks were laid in a herringbone in the spandrels, the triangles of wall that fill the space beside the curve of an arch, which he would have liked, because he liked a pattern. I told him about the girl. I told him about Yalda, about the pomegranates, about the green book, about gham makhor. I told him about the little red book in my pocket and the line in Persian I couldn’t read. I asked him what it said. He didn’t know either. He had never been to Iran. He had been to Italy once on his honeymoon and to Austria many times and that was all, and he would have hated it here, he would have complained about the tea, and he would have loved it.

I told him I was going to die. I said it to him very plainly, the way he always talked to me. I said, Papa, I’m going to die here. Under a guesthouse in Bam. Under a good arch. I said, You told me to go and see something. I went.

And he didn’t say anything. He was never a talker. He just sat there in my head in the dark, the way he’d sat in his chair by the window in the evenings, not saying anything, being there. I was glad of him.
And then, sometime in the night, the deep part of the night, I heard her.

I want to say this carefully. I am a conservator. I am a scientist, of a kind. I measure things for a living. I know what thirst does, and cold, and the dark, and being trapped, and grief, and what all of those together can do to a mind lying alone under a fallen building for twenty hours. I have read about it since. Many people who have been buried after earthquakes have heard voices. Their dead. Their mothers. God. Music. It’s well known. It’s the brain, starved of everything it needs, filling the dark with what it wants most. I know all of this.
I am going to tell you what I heard anyway.

I heard a girl’s voice. Very close. As if she were lying beside me on the floor of the passage, on my right, in the gap where the air came in, with her face a hand’s width from my face. Not loud. Soft, and clear, and steady, the way you speak to someone in a bed beside you at night so as not to wake the house.
She was reciting the poem.
Yusof-e gomgashteh bāz āyad be Kan’ān, gham makhor.

I knew it at once. I didn’t know the words, but I knew the music of it, the rise and the fall, the way it went up on Kan’ān and came down to rest on gham makhor at the end of the line like a bird landing on a branch. I had heard it once, by lamplight, at Yalda, in that same voice.
Kolbeh-ye ahzān shavad ruzi golestān, gham makhor.

She went on. Line after line. The whole poem. I didn’t know how many lines there were. I didn’t know any of the words except the two that came back at the end of every line, over and over, like a heartbeat. Gham makhor. Gham makhor. The voice was patient. It didn’t hurry. When it got to the end it went back to the beginning, the way the stories had gone round and round at Yalda, the way you sing a child to sleep.

And then, after the second time through, it stopped. And in the silence, close to my face, the voice said, in English. Careful English. Schoolgirl English, with each word set down by itself like a small building:
“Don’t be sad, Clara. Wait. Someone is coming. You have a good accent.”
I said, “Narges?”
My voice came out as a rasp. It hurt. I said it again.
“Narges? Are you here? Are you under here?”
Nothing. The cold breath of the qanat on my face. Far away, a dog. The rubble ticking and settling over my head.

I thought, she’s under here too. She came to meet me. She came to the guesthouse to get me, because for once in her life she had decided not to be late, because the sun has no excuse, and the house fell on her too, and she’s lying somewhere near me in the dark, hurt, and she’s trying to keep me going.
I said, “Narges, are you hurt?”
Nothing.

So I did the only thing I could think of. I said the only Persian I was sure of, the thing she’d taught me. The thing she said was the most important thing in Persian. I said it into the dark, toward the gap where the air came in, with my lips cracking:
“Gham makhor.”
And then again. And again. Until I couldn’t anymore.

Nobody answered. But I wasn’t afraid anymore, after that. I don’t know how else to say it. Something had sat down beside me in the dark and stayed there. I lay with my cheek on the cold floor and my face toward the gap and the breath of the old water on my lips, and I said gham makhor to it, over and over, very quietly, the way you’d say a word to a frightened animal, and at some point I slept.
15. The First Night Ayoub

The trucks came in the afternoon. And the people from Kerman, in cars, in pickups, in buses, with shovels, with water, with bread, driving three hours through the desert with their hazard lights on because they’d heard on the radio and couldn’t believe it and came to see. And then, as it got dark, the first helicopters, coming in low over the palms with their lights, landing in the football ground, which was the only open place left. And soldiers. And the Red Crescent, Helāl-e Ahmar [he-LAAL-eh AH-mar], in their red and white, with tents and blankets.
By night there were thousands of people in Bam who had not been there in the morning. And thousands of people in Bam who had been there in the morning and were not there anymore.

They took the dead to the cemetery on the edge of town in trucks. Open trucks, with the bodies lying in the back in their blankets, side by side, and the families running after them, or riding in the back with them, holding on. There was no time. There was no room. There was no way to wash them, the way we wash our dead, with water three times, and wrap them in white cloth, because there was no water and no white cloth and no one to do it. There were too many. The men from the government and the clerics said it was permitted, in a disaster like this, to bury without washing. They said God understands. They said the dead of Bam were martyrs, shahid [sha-HEED], and martyrs go to God as they are, in the clothes they died in, and need no washing.

They dug the graves with machines. Bulldozers. Long trenches, side by side, in the cold earth at the edge of the desert. And the dead were laid in the trenches in rows. Somebody had sense, at least, and took photographs. A man with a camera went along the rows before the earth went over them, and took a picture of each face, and wrote a number, so that afterwards people who had not been there could come and look at the pictures and find their own.
We were there. Tahereh and me. And my daughter, on the back of a truck with eleven others, in her school coat and her blanket with the birds, with the dust of Bam still on her eyelashes.

We put her in the ground at sunset. In a row. Between a man I didn’t know and a little boy. I got down into the trench myself, though they told me not to, and I took her from the men on the truck and laid her down. The earth there was the same earth as everywhere in Bam, fine and pale, the colour of a camel. The earth of my bricks. I put my hand flat on it beside her face and I thought, I don’t know why, about the way the khesht goes back to being earth when it’s finished being a wall. I thought, she’s going back. She was a wall for a little while. Now she’s earth.
It’s a thing a mud man thinks. I’m not proud of it. It didn’t help.
Tahereh threw the first handful.

I had the second in my hand. I held it a long time. It was cold, and dry, and it ran a little between my fingers, the way good earth runs before you wet it. I knew that earth. I had stood in it to my knees every working day of my life. I had made walls of it for the dead and the unborn. I could not throw it on her. So I knelt at the edge of the trench and opened my hand slowly above her, close, and let it go down onto the blanket with the birds the way you let sand go through a sieve, softly, so that it would not wake anybody.
Then the bulldozer.

That night we slept in the street. Everybody did. Nobody would go near anything that was still standing. We had a fire made from the wood of our own house, the broken beams of the big room, and the blankets the Red Crescent gave us, and we sat around the fire in the lane with our neighbour’s family and the families from three other houses, and it was so cold the frost came on the blankets, and nobody talked.

The aftershocks came all night. Every time, everyone jumped up. Everyone. A whole street of people jumping to their feet in the dark at the same moment like a flock of birds startling, and then standing there, and then sitting back down.

I had my pipe. It was in my pocket. I don’t know why; I must have picked it up out of the rubble without thinking, the way you pick up your keys. I had the little brass box with my taryāk in it. I had charcoal from the fire.
I smoked. All night. All of it. Everything I had.
I want to tell you what opium does, because you will need to know, later, to understand what happened to me.

It takes the pain away. That’s the first thing. Not just the pain in your back, or your legs, though it does that. It takes the other pain too. It doesn’t remove it. It puts it in another room. You can still hear it through the wall, but it’s in another room, and you are sitting in this room, warm, and the edges of everything are soft, and you are a little bit outside yourself, watching yourself from a corner of the ceiling, and the man you’re watching is very sad, poor man, but it’s not you, exactly. That’s what it does. That’s why we smoke it in Kerman. That’s why, after Bam, so many more of us smoked it than before. Half the town, they said later. Men and women. Old people. Young people. Everybody had something in another room they needed to keep there.

The second thing it does, if you take enough, and you haven’t slept, and you’re very cold, and you’ve been digging with your hands for twelve hours, and you’ve buried your daughter in a trench, is it opens a door. Things come through the door. Pictures. Voices. The line between what you’re thinking and what you’re seeing gets thin and soft, like old plaster. You’re not asleep and you’re not awake. You’re in a place between, a place like twilight, where the dead aren’t quite dead and the living aren’t quite alive and everything is very calm and very slow and very far away.
That night by the fire, in that place, I saw the Arg.

Not the heap. The Arg. Standing. Whole. On its rock, against the stars, with all its towers, gold, the way it looks in the last of the sun. Walls and towers and the castle at the top with the square tower on it. And all along the top of the wall, the highest wall, of the castle, there were people standing. Hundreds of them, in a long line, quiet, looking out over the town. Men and women and children. I couldn’t see their faces. They were only shapes against the stars. But I knew they were everyone. Everyone from that morning. Standing on the wall of the castle, waiting for the sun.
I looked for her among them. A tall thin shape, in a long coat. I couldn’t find her.
Then I looked for the German woman. I couldn’t find her either.

And then the neighbour’s wife put another beam on the fire and the sparks went up, and the Arg was a heap of earth again against the stars, and I was sitting in the street in the cold with the pipe gone out in my hand.
From Under the City
Let me tell you what I did. Plainly. I owe you that. I don’t apologise, but I don’t hide either.

Under your town, a few kilometres down, which is shallow, as these things go, there is a crack in me running north and south. Your scientists had drawn a fault on their maps here, a long line in the land, but they had drawn it a little way to the east, out past the edge of the town, where it shows itself on the surface as a long low ridge. They thought that was where I was cracked. They were partly right. The crack they’d drawn is real. But I had another, a younger one, a branch, running right under the houses, under the old town, under the new town, under the guesthouse with the orange tree and the mud man’s courtyard and the girl’s white room. It didn’t show itself on the surface. Nobody had seen it. It didn’t appear on any map. That’s not a crime. It’s only what I am. I don’t explain myself to surveyors.

On the fifth morning after the longest night, at twenty-six minutes and fifty-two seconds past five, the strain in that hidden crack, the strain that had been building for longer than your people have been building houses, became more than the rock could hold. And the rock broke.

It broke a little to the south of the town and tore upward and northward, straight toward the houses and in under them, faster than a bullet, for something like fifteen kilometres. One side of me slid past the other. Not far. About the length of a man lying down. But all at once. And because the break began so shallow, and so close, right under the houses, and because it ran toward the town as it broke, the shaking came up into Bam with a force that almost never happens. Straight up. As hard as the pull of the earth itself. Things on the ground were thrown into the air. Roofs were lifted and dropped. A heavy roof, lifted off its walls and dropped back onto them, does not land where it was. The walls go sideways. The roof goes down.
It lasted twelve seconds, or thereabouts. That’s all I did. Twelve seconds. Then I was finished, and I lay still.
Everything that happened after that, you did.
I’m not saying that to be cruel. I’m not anything. I’m saying it because you should know the shape of it.

The old mud houses fell. Many of them. They were old, and some had been badly patched, and their clay was dry and weak, and some had heavy roofs of earth laid over beams, and the beams were eaten by termites. But a mud house that falls is soft. It breaks into earth. A man can dig out of it with his hands, and many did, and many were dug out, breathing, by their neighbours.

The domes held, more often than not. A dome takes the weight and sends it round and down into the walls, all the way round. An arch is the same. Your ancestors learned that from me, from the shape of caves, a long time ago.

The new houses fell harder. That is what your engineers found, afterwards, when they came and walked through the rubble with their notebooks and measured everything. Not only the new houses killed; many old houses had heavy roofs of earth on rotten beams, and those killed too. But a great many of the dead in this town died in buildings less than thirty years old. Houses of fired brick with flat heavy roofs of concrete and steel laid on top, roofs not tied to their walls, steel too thin, too little of it, built without anyone checking, built the way the man down the street built. When those walls were thrown sideways, the roofs came straight down, whole. A roof of concrete doesn’t break into earth. It stays a roof. It comes down on you in one piece, the weight of a truck, and no neighbour can lift it, and there’s no air under it.

The citadel on the rock fell too. It was old and dry and patched and eaten by insects, and it had stood for a very long time, and its time came. I won’t pretend I’m sorry about the citadel. It was mine before it was yours. It’s mine again now. Your people will build it up again. They always do. That’s the nature of your people and of clay: you agree, for a while, to be walls together, and then you let go, and then you agree again.
If you want it short, the way your children want things short, here it is:
I held my breath for a thousand years under your weddings, under your tears; then twelve heartbeats long I let it go, and the walls came down, and the roofs came low.
The mud fell soft and could be dug, the dome held round like a mother’s hug, the palm bent low and stood again, but the stone lid fell whole on the children of men.
I’ll tell you one more thing, because you’re wondering about the woman under the arch, and the voice.

I don’t know about the voice. I’m earth. Earth doesn’t speak, except here, to you, and only because you’ve leaned down. I can tell you what I carried that night. I carried the breath of the old water up the stone steps into the rubble, the way it had breathed up and down those steps for three hundred years. I carried the cold. I carried a German woman’s knocking on an arch, three and three and three, until her knuckles bled, out into the rubble where nobody could hear it over all the other knocking.
And I carried, that night, from somewhere, a girl’s voice saying a poem.

I’m not going to tell you where it came from. I’ve told you I don’t apologise. I also don’t explain. The girl was in me by sunset, in a trench at the edge of the desert, with the dust of my own body on her eyelashes. Everything that goes into me, I keep.
Whether I gave something back, that night, under the arch, you’ll have to decide for yourself. That’s how it is with me. That’s how it has always been.
IV. THE TENTS
16. Time Without Edges Clara
I lost the days.

That’s the simplest way to say it. Under the arch, in the dark, time stopped being a line and became a room I was lying in. I could tell day from night, at first, by the grey stain of light to my right and by the depth of the cold. Then I couldn’t. I would wake and not know if I had slept an hour or a day. I would see the grey light and think it was dawn, and watch it, and it would go darker, and I’d understand it had been dusk. Or I’d think it was still the first night and then realise my lips had cracked open in a new place, and the pain in my legs had changed again, and that something had gone by that I had not been present for.

My watch had a light on it, a little green glow if you pressed the button. I pressed it, at first, every few minutes. Then I couldn’t bear to. Then I forgot it was there. Later I understood that I had been under the arch for something like a hundred hours. I can only tell you that it was one long thing, without edges, like being held underwater in the dark.

Thirst is a person. I want to say that and I know it sounds mad. After the first day it was not a feeling, it was someone in there with me, lying on top of me, with its mouth on my mouth. Thirst has a voice. It talks to you all the time, in a dry whisper, about water. Glasses of water. Taps. Rain. The fountain in the square in Regensburg where I used to put my hands in summer as a child. The long pool in the courtyard of the guesthouse, with the orange tree reflected in it. The cold water of the qanat, running clear as air over the pebbles in the dark, a few metres below me, just under the floor, so close I could smell it on every breath.

I licked the wall. I’m not ashamed. In the mornings, near the gap where the qanat’s breath came in, the cold made a faint dampness on the plaster beside my face, and I put my tongue against it and took what there was. It tasted of earth. I did it every time I woke. It wasn’t enough to swallow. It was enough to remember swallowing.

I urinated where I lay, after the first day, because there was nothing else to do. I don’t need to describe that. I mention it because the people who rescue you always ask, very gently, and it’s better to say it once, plainly, and be done.
On the second day, or the third, the visions started properly.

I want to describe them, because they were beautiful, and because I’ve read since about what thirst and cold and the dark do to the brain, and the reading doesn’t take away from the beauty. It only explains it. When your body runs out of water, your blood gets thicker, and less of it gets to your brain, and less oxygen with it. When you lie in the dark, with nothing to see, the part of your brain that makes sight starts making sight on its own, out of nothing, the way a radio between stations makes a hiss. When you’re very cold, and very frightened, and very tired, all of those things together loosen the walls between what you remember and what you see. The doctor in Germany called it a kind of delirium. I’ve also read that the same things happen to monks in caves, and to people lost in deserts, and to sailors adrift, and that some of them come back and say they saw God, and some of them come back and say they saw their mothers, and some of them come back and say nothing at all for the rest of their lives.
I saw the Arg.

Not as it was the afternoon I’d sat on its wall and made my notes. I saw it at every age at once. I saw it rising. I saw men treading mud in pits at the foot of the rock, hundreds of them, barefoot, in the heat, with straw in the mud, the way Ayoub trod it. I saw them lift the bricks in the wooden frames and lay them in the sun in rows, thousands of rows, so many bricks drying in the sun that the ground around the rock was a chessboard of them out to the palms. I saw the walls go up, course on course, and the towers rise, and the castle climb the rock in terraces. I saw it finished, gold against the sky. Then I saw it worn: the rains of a hundred winters softening its edges, the walls slumping a little, the towers losing their tops. I saw men come and patch it. I saw soldiers on the walls, archers, Afghans riding in over the desert in a cloud of dust, smoke, the walls breached and repaired. I saw caravans. Long lines of camels coming in from the desert under the walls with bells round their necks, swaying, loaded with silk and spice and indigo, and the camel drivers in dusty turbans looking up at the towers with relief, the way I had looked up at them from the bus. I saw the town empty, a hundred and fifty years ago, everybody moving out of the old walls and down into the new town below, and the Arg left alone on its rock to the wind and the pigeons, falling slowly, a little each year.

I saw all of that in the dark, under the arch, as clearly as I see this page. It went by like a film run very fast. Then it went by again, slowly. Then it stopped, and the Arg stood on its rock in the gold light, and on the top wall of the castle, in a long line against the sky, there were people standing. Waiting for the sun.
I looked for her among them. I couldn’t find her.

And I heard the voice. Every night, I think, though I’m not sure how many nights there were. The girl’s voice, close, on my right, in the gap where the air came in. Reciting the poem. The whole poem, slowly, the music of it going up and coming down to rest on gham makhor. Then back to the beginning.
I said gham makhor to it, when I could. My lips were split and my tongue was dry as leather and I could hardly shape the words. I said them anyway.
I didn’t hear her speak English again. Only the first night. Only once.
Don’t be sad, Clara. Wait. Someone is coming.

There was a long time, toward the end, when I didn’t hear anything. Not the voice, not the town. The digging had moved away. The voices outside had changed; there were more of them, and stranger, machines, engines, heavy things moving, once a helicopter very low over my head, so loud the rubble shivered and earth trickled onto my neck, and once, far off, a dog barking in a way that wasn’t like the town dogs, a short, sharp, trained bark, and men’s voices calling to it in a language that was not Persian. I knocked. I knocked with the flat of my hand. I knocked until I couldn’t lift my hand.
Then there was a long time when I was nowhere.

I don’t mean I was asleep. I mean there was nobody in me to be anywhere. I was the dark. I was the cold. I was the arch, holding. I was the floor. I don’t know how to say it better than that. I think I was very close to dying. I think I knew it, in the way you know things in a dream, without fear. I remember thinking, quite calmly, that I was becoming part of the house. That in a while I would be the same temperature as the floor and the same colour as the dust, and then there would be no difference between me and the earth at all, and the girl had been right about everything, and it was all just going back, khesht to earth, the way it always goes.
And it was fine. That’s the strangest thing I can tell you. Down there, at the very bottom, it was fine.
And then, from somewhere below me, from somewhere under the floor, in the dark, I heard a man’s voice.
17. The Planes Ayoub
On the third day, the twenty-eighth, they found an old man alive.

Seventy-something. A grandfather. Under his house, four lanes from ours, under a heap of khesht, in a little space beside his bed where a beam had fallen on a cupboard and made a roof. Alive. Thirsty. Calm. A rescue team from abroad found him with a dog. When they lifted him out, people say, he asked for tea.

I heard about it from my neighbour. He said the whole street went to look. I didn’t go. I was sitting in the tent the Red Crescent had given us, on the main road, a white canvas tent in a long row of white canvas tents, with Tahereh lying beside me with her face to the canvas, not sleeping. I was looking at the pen.

Dark green. German. Heavy, for its size. A gold nib. Made in Germany along the side in small letters. I had taken it out of her pocket in the courtyard on the first morning, and I’d been holding it ever since. I held it at the grave. I held it all night by the fire. I’d been holding it for two days. I didn’t know whose it was. I knew it was not hers. I knew that she had put it in the pocket over her heart and buttoned the pocket, which she never did with anything, and that she had been holding her hand over it when she died.

Tahereh knew. On the second day, without turning round from the canvas, she said, “The German gave it to her. On Christmas. For her translations. She told me.” Then she didn’t say anything else for a day.
The world came. I want to tell you about that, because it was strange, and because you won’t believe it unless someone tells you who was there.

On the second day the teams from other countries started arriving. They flew into Kerman and drove the three hours in buses and trucks, with their machines and their dogs and their tents and their uniforms in colours we had never seen. Swiss in red. Germans in orange. Japanese in blue. Turks. Russians. French. Chinese. Men from forty countries, they said. Bam’s little airport, with its control tower cracked down the middle, took planes all day and all night, big grey planes, the roar of them going over the tents, over the palms, so low you could see the rivets.
And on the fifth day, the planes from America.

I was there when the first one came down. I was standing at the fence of the airport with my neighbour, and the plane came in low over the desert, enormous, grey, with its four engines roaring and the American star painted on its side, and everyone along the fence stopped and watched it. Nobody said anything. A man beside me said, very quietly, under his breath, Āmrikā [aam-ree-KAA]. America. As if he couldn’t believe the word.

You have to understand. Since the revolution, since 1979, since the embassy, twenty-four years, America was the enemy. The Great Satan, they called it, on the walls of every city, in the prayers on Friday. Since the spring of 1980, when American helicopters came down burning in the desert near Tabas trying to rescue the embassy hostages, no American military plane had landed in Iran. Nearly half my life. And here it was, a great grey American military plane, landing at the little airport outside a town that wasn’t there anymore, and the back of it opening, and men in American uniforms coming down the ramp carrying boxes of medicine and blankets and water, and looking around at Bam, at the heaps of earth and the white tents and the grey people standing along the fence, with the same face everyone wore who came to Bam for the first time. The face of a man who has walked into a room where something terrible has happened and doesn’t know where to put his eyes.

Some people at the fence clapped. Some spat. Most of them just watched. On the radio that night, the state radio, a man said that America was using the tragedy of Bam to meddle in Iran’s affairs. On the same radio, an hour later, another man thanked all the nations of the world, by name, including America. That’s Iran. Both things, on the same radio, on the same night.

They brought tents, and water, and blankets, and a field hospital, and everyone said the Germans had the best one. They brought machines that could lift the concrete roofs. They brought dogs that could smell a living person under ten metres of rubble.
My neighbour said to me, on the fourth day, “Ayoub. They have machines. They can lift the slab off your kitchen. They can get her things. Her books.”
I said, “She doesn’t need her books.”
He looked at me for a long time.
“You haven’t slept,” he said. “Since. Have you?”
I didn’t answer.
“You’re smoking too much,” he said. “Everybody is. I am. But you’re smoking too much.”
I didn’t answer that either.
I’ll tell you the truth about those days, because I promised I would.

I didn’t sleep. I couldn’t. When I lay down and closed my eyes I was on the slab with my ear to the concrete, listening. So I didn’t lie down. I sat up in the tent with the pen in my hand, or I walked the town in the dark, over the rubble, past the fires, past the families sitting around them, past the rows of tents, past the dogs and the foreigners and their lights and their machines, up the hill to the foot of what had been the Arg, and stood there, looking up at the heap.

And I smoked. Every time I could. Taryāk was easy to get, those days. Easier than water. Men went round the tents with it. Some of them sold it. Some of them gave it away. Some of them were from the government, people said, and some were not, and nobody asked. It came in from the east, over the desert, the way it had always come, and after Bam it came faster. People said the government was turning a blind eye, to keep people calm. People said a lot of things. I didn’t care. I smoked it. It put the slab in another room.

And in that other room, in that soft, slow, twilight place where the opium takes you when you have not slept for three days, the line between the living and the dead was very thin. Thinner than plaster. I saw things. I’m telling you. I saw the people on the wall of the castle every night. I saw my father, treading mud. I heard my daughter.
I heard her reciting.

Every time I closed my eyes, in that place, I heard her voice, very close, saying the poem she had read for the German at Yalda. Yusof-e gomgashteh. The whole thing. Again and again. Gham makhor. Gham makhor. Don’t grieve. Don’t eat sorrow.
I ate it. Every bite. I’m not a poet. I’m a mud man.
18. The Mother Well Ayoub
On the night of the twenty-ninth, I went down into the qanat.
I’ll tell you why. I don’t have a good reason. I have only the true one.

I went because I couldn’t bear to be above ground anymore. Above ground was the slab, and the tents, and the trenches at the edge of the desert, and the heap where the Arg had been, and the eyes of my wife, who still had not turned round from the canvas. Above ground everything was broken and grey and lit by foreigners’ floodlights all night long and full of the sound of engines and dogs and people crying. And I thought of the place where none of that was. The place under all of it. Where the water was still running in the dark the way it always ran, going home, not caring about anything. The mother, under the children.
I wanted to be there. That’s all. I wanted to sit by the water in the dark where it was quiet, and smoke, and listen to it, and not be anywhere.

There was a shaft the old man had shown me when I was a boy, in a garden at the edge of the old town, near the guesthouse quarter. One of the well-shafts of the big qanat that ran under that part of Bam, the old qanat, the one that fed the gardens below the Arg. It had iron rungs set into the side, put there sixty years ago by the muqanni who looked after that stretch, so that he could climb down to clear it. The old man used to take me there in summer, without telling anybody, and we would climb down together and sit at the bottom with our feet in the water to get out of the heat. He said it was the coolest place in Bam, and the oldest, and the only place where you could hear what the earth was thinking.

I found the garden in the dark, though the walls around it were down. The palms in it were standing. The shaft was still there. A ring of earth, a black hole in the middle, the same as always. I put my hand down and found the first rung. It was cold and solid. The shaft had not collapsed. The earthquake had knocked down every house in Bam and it had not knocked down a hole in the ground.

I had a torch, one of the foreigners’ torches from the tent, a heavy black one with a strong white light. I had my pipe and my box of taryāk in my coat. I had the pen in my pocket, the inside one, on the left. I climbed down.
At the bottom I sat in the dark beside the water, and turned off the torch, and smoked.

It was very quiet. Quieter than anywhere I had ever been. The noise of the town above was gone, swallowed by the earth, and all there was was the water, chuckling in its channel in the dark, and a drop falling somewhere up the tunnel, slow, slow, like a clock, and my own breath. It was cold, but a different cold from above, a wet, old, still cold, like the inside of a well. Which it was. The opium went into me and the dark went soft and I sat there a long time and didn’t think about anything.
And then I heard her.

Not her. I know now. I’m telling you what I thought. In that dark, in that place, in that soft room where the opium had put me, I heard my daughter reciting the poem, the way I’d been hearing it every time I closed my eyes for three days. Yusof-e gomgashteh. And I started saying it with her. Out loud. I don’t know why. My voice went off down the tunnel in the dark, low, rough, the voice of a man who hasn’t slept or spoken for three days, saying the poem to the water.
Yusof-e gomgashteh bāz āyad be Kan’ān, gham makhor.
Kolbeh-ye ahzān shavad ruzi golestān, gham makhor.

I said the whole thing. I said it again. I got up, I don’t know why. And before I moved, I did what the old man taught me when I was nine. I took a match from my pocket and struck it and held it out into the dark of the tunnel at arm’s length. A flame before a foot. It burned tall and yellow. The air was good. The earthquake had shaken the tunnel and dropped its roof in places, but it had not poisoned it. I shook the match out and put it in my pocket, because you don’t leave anything in a qanat, and the old man would have cuffed me.

Then I started to walk, bent over, along the tunnel, downstream, in the dark, with my hand on the wall, saying it. Following the water. The water goes home. I followed it. I said the poem to it as I walked, line after line, gham makhor, gham makhor, the way you’d say it to a child you were carrying in the dark, the way she’d said it to the German at Yalda.

The tunnel went on. Under the old town. Under the gardens, under the lanes, under the fallen houses. In places the roof had come down a little, a slope of earth across the floor, and I climbed over it on my hands and knees. In places I could see light above me, a faint grey square, where another well-shaft went up to the surface, and I could hear, very faintly, far above, the engines and the dogs. Then the dark again. And the water. And my voice.

I counted the shafts. I didn’t decide to; my body did it, the way the old man taught me, the way every muqanni does, because underground the shafts are the only map. One grey square, the garden where I’d come down. Two, the edge of the old bazaar. Three, four, the lanes behind the mosque. I knew this qanat. I had walked it at nine and ten and eleven with my hand in an old man’s belt. Five. Six. The old merchants’ quarter, the houses with their own stairs down to the water. I knew where I was under my town better than I had ever known it from on top.

I said, Agar seil-e fanā bonyād-e hasti bar kanad [a-GAR SEIL-eh fa-NAA bon-YAAD-eh has-TEE bar ka-NAD]. The line about the flood. If the flood of annihilation tears up the foundation of everything that is. Chun to rā Nuh ast kashtibān [CHOON to RAA NOOH ast kash-tee-BAAN], while you have Noah, Nuh, for your captain, ze tufān gham makhor [ze too-FAAN GHAM ma-KHOR]. Don’t grieve over the storm.
And somewhere ahead of me, in the dark, very faint, a voice said:
“Gham makhor.”
I stopped. I stood in the tunnel bent over with my hand on the wall and the water running past my feet. I didn’t breathe.

It was a woman’s voice. Not my daughter’s. I knew it was not my daughter’s the moment I heard it, even in the opium, even in the dark. It was older. It was cracked and dry and so weak it was hardly a voice at all, a scrape of breath with the shape of words in it. And it was wrong. The gh was wrong, too soft, and the kh was wrong, too hard, a foreign throat trying to make a Persian sound.
“Gham makhor,” it said again. From ahead. From somewhere above the tunnel, ahead and above, in the dark.

I knew that accent. I had heard it on Yalda night, in my grandfather’s room, by the lamp, saying merci to my sisters. I had heard it say gham makhor when my daughter taught it, with a crack in it, on the edge of crying.
I turned on the torch.

The tunnel ran straight ahead for twenty metres, and then on the left side of it, there was an opening. A doorway in the earth, an arch cut into the wall, and steps going up out of it. Old steps, cut into the ground, steep and narrow, worn in the middle by three hundred years of women coming down with jars for water. A pāyāb. The stairs from a house down to the qanat.

The steps went up into the dark, twenty of them or a few more, and stopped. At the top there was rubble. Earth and brick, jammed into the stairway where the house above had fallen into it. But not all the way. At the top, on one side, there was a gap. A black hole, the size of a man’s head, between the fallen bricks and the old arch of the stairway roof.

I knew where I was. I’d been walking under the old town toward the Arg. This was the pāyāb of the old merchant’s house four lanes from mine. The house with the long pool and the orange tree. The guesthouse.
I climbed the steps. I put my face to the gap. I shone the torch into it.

Rubble. Dust. A slope of fallen earth and brick going up, and on the right, a curve of plaster: an arch, cracked across, holding. And under the arch, lying on her face on the floor of a passage, with her cheek on the stone and her head turned toward me, toward the gap, toward the light, a woman. Her hair was grey with dust. Her face was grey with dust. Her lips were black and split. Her eyes were closed. Her right hand was lying flat on the floor in front of her face, palm down, and the knuckles of it were black with old blood.
I said her name the way I said it. Kelaara.
