Her eyes opened. In the light of the torch they were the bluest thing I had ever seen. Blue as the tiles on the mosque. They looked straight at me. They didn’t understand anything. Then her lips moved, and no sound came out, and then they moved again and the sound came, the scrape of breath with the shape of words in it.
“Gham makhor.”

I don’t remember all of what came next. I know I dug. With my hands, at the gap, pulling bricks back into the stairway and letting them fall down the steps behind me into the water. I know I talked to her the whole time, in Persian, she didn’t understand a word, I said I’m here, I’m here, I’m Ayoub, it’s Ayoub, the mud man, wait, wait. I know at some point I put my arm through the gap up to the shoulder and found her hand, and it was so cold it was like holding a stone, and her fingers closed on mine, very slightly. I know I couldn’t move what was on her legs. I know I went back down the steps and along the tunnel and up the rungs of the old man’s shaft into the cold night and ran, ran, over the rubble, in the dark, shouting, to the nearest of the foreigners’ lights, and that the men there were German, in orange, with a dog, and I couldn’t speak a word of their language and they couldn’t speak a word of mine, and I grabbed one of them by the front of his orange coat and said the only German word I knew, which was a word she had taught me, by my mixing pit, touching my mud.
Lehm. Clay. Earth.
And then I pointed at the ground, and said, in English, my forty words, Woman. German. Alive. Under.

It took them four hours to get her out. They didn’t go through the qanat. They came from above, the way rescuers do, with their machines and their jacks and their careful voices, cutting down through the rubble of the guesthouse toward the arch while one of them, a big man with a red beard, lay on his stomach in the pāyāb with his face at the gap where mine had been, and talked to her in German the whole time. I sat on the steps below him, in the dark, with my feet in the water of the qanat. I held her hand through the gap until they told me to let go so they could get her legs free. Then I sat on the steps and listened to the man with the red beard talking to her in her own language, gently, steadily, the way she had needed someone to talk to her for four days, and I didn’t understand a word of it, and I didn’t need to.

When they brought her up, it was dawn. The sun was coming up over the mountains, red, enormous, through the dust, the way it always comes up over Bam. The thirtieth of December. I stood in the rubble of the guesthouse and watched them carry her past me on a stretcher, wrapped in a silver blanket that crackled, with a tube in her arm and a mask on her face.

As they went past, she turned her head on the stretcher and looked at me with those blue eyes, and lifted the hand with the black knuckles, a little, and touched the mask, as if she wanted to say something.
They kept walking. I stood there. The sun came up.
I took the pen out of my pocket and held it in my hand.
19. Light Clara
The first thing I saw was the sun.

They brought me up through a hole they had cut in the rubble, on a board, on my back, and the first thing I saw was the sky, and it was full of red light. The sun was coming up. I had been under the arch for four days and two hours, they told me afterwards, and I came out at sunrise, and the sky was red and gold and the dust in the air turned it into fire, and I lay on the board and looked at it and I could not close my eyes against it. A man had to put his hand over them.
The man with the red beard said, in German, You’re out. You’re out. You’re out. Clara. You’re out. He said my name. He knew my name. How did he know my name?
Ayoub, I learned later. Ayoub told them, in English, Kelaara.

They flew me to Kerman in a helicopter, and kept me there two days, and then flew me to Tehran, and from Tehran, three days later, to Munich, in another plane, a military one, the German one, with a doctor sitting beside me the whole way holding the bag of fluid that was going into my arm. My legs were very bad. The left one they saved. The right one, below the knee, they couldn’t. I’m telling you that the way the surgeon told me, without any adjectives, because adjectives don’t help. I walk well now, with the new one. I walk on scaffolding. I climb ladders. You wouldn’t know, unless you saw me take off my boot.

I was glad. I want to say that clearly, because people never believe it. When the surgeon told me, in Munich, standing at the foot of the bed with his hands behind his back, I said, Is that all? He thought I was in shock. I wasn’t. I’d been lying in the dark for four days becoming the same temperature as the floor. A leg is not much, against that. A leg is a fair price.
Before they flew me out of Kerman, Ayoub came to the hospital.

He’d come three hours across the desert in his neighbour’s pickup, with the neighbour driving, and a nurse in the hospital who spoke English came with him to my bed, and stood between us, and translated.

He looked terrible. I suppose I did too. He was grey all over, grey dust in the creases of his face and his hands, and his eyes were red and sunk deep in his head, and his hands shook. He’d brought me a bag of dates. Bam dates, the black soft ones, a little crushed, wrapped in a newspaper. He put them on the table beside the bed and stood there with his hands at his sides, not knowing where to look.
I said, “Narges?”

He looked at the nurse. The nurse looked at me. She didn’t need to say anything. I knew from her face before she opened her mouth. I knew from his. I think I had known since the first night. I think I’d known since the voice.
“She died in the earthquake,” the nurse said, very gently. “In her room. Her father found her that morning.”
“When?”
The nurse asked him. He said something short.
“At the moment,” the nurse said. “At five twenty-six. She was dressed to go out. To meet you.”
I told him about the voice.
I didn’t plan to. I didn’t know if it was right. I just told him. The nurse translated, slowly, sentence by sentence, and I watched his face while she did it.

I said that the first night, the first night under the arch, before anyone could have been down in the qanat, before he could have been anywhere, I’d heard a girl’s voice close beside me, reciting the poem from Yalda. The whole poem. Twice. And that then, in English, careful English, the voice had said, Don’t be sad, Clara. Wait. Someone is coming. You have a good accent.
The nurse stopped translating at You have a good accent and looked at me. I nodded. She said it to him.

He stood there. He didn’t move for a long time. Then he sat down, very suddenly, on the edge of the chair by the bed, as if his legs had gone. He put his face in his hands. Then he took his hands away and looked at me, and said something to the nurse, very quietly.

“He says,” said the nurse, “he went down into the qanat on the fourth night. Only the fourth night. He says he was reciting that poem in the tunnel. He says he heard you answer him. He says that’s how he found you.”
“I know,” I said. “I heard him. On the last night. A man’s voice. Under the floor.”

“He says,” said the nurse, and then she stopped, and asked him something, and he answered, and she looked at him for a while before she turned back to me. “He says he was not there on the first night. He says on the first night he was in the street, by a fire, with his wife and his neighbours. He says on the first night he buried her.”
He took something out of his pocket and put it on the blanket beside my hand.
The green pen.
I looked at it. I didn’t touch it.

“He says it was in her coat,” said the nurse. “Over her heart. In the pocket, buttoned. Her hand was on it. He says he didn’t know whose it was. His wife told him.” She listened to him for a moment more. “He says it belongs to you. He says it should go back to you.”

I picked it up. It was warm from his pocket. I held it for a while. Then I put it back in his hand, and closed his fingers over it, his cracked grey fingers, with my own, the hand with the black knuckles.
“No,” I said. “Tell him no. Tell him it’s hers. Tell him I gave it to her for her translations. Tell him somebody has to finish them.”
The nurse told him.
He looked at the pen in his hand. Then he put it back in the inside pocket of his coat, on the left, over his heart, and buttoned the pocket, and put his hand flat over it.

I knew that gesture. I had seen it on Christmas morning, in a lane in Bam, on a girl running to school with her coat flying. He could not have known that. Nobody had told him. And yet there it was, his cracked grey hand pressed flat over his heart, exactly where hers had been, exactly the way. I looked at it and could not look away. I thought: this is how the dead stay. Not in voices in the dark. In our hands, doing what theirs did, without our knowing. He stood like that for a while, and I lay like that, and the nurse looked out of the window, and nobody said anything, and it was the first time since the arch that I did not feel alone.
20. Tents Ayoub

We lived in the tent for nine months. Then in a metal box, a prefabricated room, two metres by three, with a door and a window and a roof that roared in the rain and baked in the sun, for two years after that. That’s how long it took. That’s Bam.
I’m not going to tell you about all of it. I’ll tell you the shape of it.

The cold came first. That first January was the coldest anyone could remember, or it felt that way, with nothing between you and the desert night but canvas. People died of the cold, after, who had lived through the earthquake. Old people. Babies. Then the cold went, and the spring came, and the heat began, and the tents became ovens, and people sat outside them in what shade they could find, under the palms, which were all still standing, and waited. For the government. For the money. For the bulldozers to clear the lanes. For somebody to tell them what would happen next.
The whole town was a waiting room, for two years. Seventy thousand people, or a hundred thousand, nobody knew the number, sitting among the rubble of their houses in tents and boxes, waiting.

The children went back to school in tents. Five thousand of them were orphans, they said. Five thousand children who had lost their mother or their father or both in twelve seconds. Ten thousand schoolchildren were dead, they said. More than a thousand teachers. Narges’s whole class. I mean that. Of the girls in her year, at her school, so few were left that they put the rest in with the year below.
And the opium. I said I’d tell you the truth.

It came in like the tide. Before the earthquake, Bam had more than its share; it was on the road from Afghanistan, and the desert was full of men on camels and motorbikes carrying it west. After the earthquake, everybody smoked. Men who had never touched it. Women. Old women who had lost their sons sat in their tents with a vāfur and a manqal. Young men who had lost everything sat in rows at night by the fires with their eyes half closed. It was cheaper than bread. It was easier to find than water. It put the slab in the other room, and everybody had a slab.

Doctors came, and counsellors from Tehran with notebooks, and sat in tents and tried to get people to talk about it. Some people talked. Most people smoked. In the evenings, at the tent camp, the sweet heavy smell of it hung over the rows of white canvas like the smell of the dates in autumn used to hang over the town. People made jokes about it. Bam always smelled sweet, they said. Before, dates. Now, this.

I smoked it all that winter and all that spring. Every day. I’m not going to pretend otherwise. Tahereh didn’t say anything. She had stopped saying anything to me at all. We lay in the tent at night with our backs to each other and the cold between us and I smoked until the room went soft and I could hear my daughter reciting.
I stopped in the summer. I’ll tell you how, later. It wasn’t anything brave.
And the talk. In the tents, at night, around the fires, there was nothing to do but talk. And everybody talked about the same thing. Why.
Why Bam. Why so many. Why my house. Why my child. Why the new buildings and not the old ones. Why the help took so long. Why the money didn’t come.
I’ll tell you what they said. All of it, the sensible and the mad. I won’t tell you which was which. I wasn’t sure myself, for a long time. I’m still not sure about some of it.

They said the aid was being stolen. That’s the first thing everybody said. The world had sent millions. Planes and planes of it, tents and blankets and food and medicine and money. Everyone had seen the planes. And yet in the camps, people said, they were sleeping in the cold with one blanket, and waiting in lines for hours for a bag of rice, and the shops in Kerman were selling foreign blankets, foreign tents, foreign tins of food with foreign writing on them, at the full price. People said it went to the officials. To their cousins. To the bazaar. People said some of it went to Tehran and never came back. People said you had to know somebody to get a prefabricated box, and the people who knew somebody got two.

They said the number was a lie. The government said twenty-six thousand dead, then thirty, then forty-three, then thirty-one, then other numbers, a different number every month, it seemed. People said the real number was twice as much. Three times. That they had buried people in trenches with no names and no photographs, whole families with nobody left to say who they were, and those were not counted. That the government wanted the number small so it would not look so bad. Or big, so the world would send more money. People believed both of these at once, sometimes in the same breath.

They said it was not God, and not the earth. They said it was a bomb. A test. That the Americans, or the Israelis, had set off something under the desert, a secret weapon, to punish Iran, to frighten it. That this was why the ground had come up and not sideways, which was not natural. That this was why the American planes had come so fast, out of guilt, to look at what they’d done. A man in our row of tents believed this with his whole heart. He’d lost his wife and three children. He would talk about it every night until somebody went and sat with him.

They said it was God. That too. A cleric came from Kerman and said in the Friday prayers in the tent mosque that disasters come when people stray from the path, and everyone knew what he meant: the opium, the smuggling, the young people with their satellite dishes and their music. Some people nodded. Some people walked out. Tahereh walked out, from the women’s side, very slowly, in the middle of the sermon, so that everybody saw. She said afterward that God had better things to do than knock down her daughter’s room because a boy in Kerman had a satellite dish.

They said the government knew. That the scientists knew there was a fault there, under Bam, and had known for years, and had told nobody, and let people go on building. That every earthquake in Iran is the same, Tabas, Rudbar, now Bam, and the government writes a book of rules every time and nobody follows the book and nobody makes them, because the people who are supposed to make them are the people who get paid not to.
And they said, quietly, the thing nobody wanted to say. They said it was us.

That the old mud houses had stood, more often than the new ones. That the people who died were mostly in the new rooms, the brick and concrete ones, with the flat roofs, the modern ones. Built by their own fathers and sons and husbands, cheaply, quickly, the way everyone built, without steel enough, without the band of concrete round the top, without an engineer, without anybody coming to look. They said it at night by the fires in low voices, not looking at anybody. Who built your room?
I built hers.
I’ve told you that already. I’ll keep telling you. I’ll tell you until you’re tired of hearing it, because I’m not tired of it, and I never will be.
But I’ll tell you something else too, because I said I’d tell you all of it. I’ll tell you what I think, now, so many years later. Not that it makes anything better.

I think all of those things were true. The aid was stolen, some of it, and some of it wasn’t, and more of it was wasted than stolen, and more of it was simply too slow. The numbers were wrong, because nobody could count, not because anybody was hiding. The government was slow, so slow, more than half a day before it even asked for help; that’s true. The rules were written and not enforced; that’s true. The scientists had drawn the fault on the wrong side of the town; that’s true too, though I don’t think they hid it. They just didn’t know. The bomb wasn’t true. I’ll tell you that later, too.

But all of those true things together, they don’t make a hand that did it. They make a shape. A shape like a crack in a wall, running from the corner of a window up toward the ceiling, at a slant, that I looked at with my nose almost touching it, three days before, and decided was the cold.
21. Bavaria Clara

In Munich it snowed all January. I lay in a hospital bed on the fourth floor and watched it come down past the window, slow and thick and grey against the grey sky, and I thought about the stars over Bam.

My mother came every day. She sat by the bed and knitted and didn’t ask me anything, which was the kindest thing she has ever done for me. My colleagues came, with flowers and German chocolates and awkward faces. A journalist came, and a nurse sent him away. Somebody from the Foreign Office came and asked me questions about the other German citizens who had been in Bam, and I told him I hadn’t known any, and he wrote that down.
At night, when the ward was quiet, I read.

I read everything about the earthquake I could find. The papers from the scientists, the seismologists, who had gone to Bam in January with their instruments and their satellites and their notebooks. I read them the way I read a report on a wall, slowly, with a pencil, underlining. I learned the words. Strike-slip: two blocks of rock sliding sideways past each other. Rupture: the break itself, racing along the fault. Surface trace: the line where a fault shows on the ground. Directivity: what happens when the break runs toward you, piling its shaking up in front of it. I learned that the fault had broken under the town, not where the maps had it, on a hidden branch nobody had seen; that the break had run toward the town as it opened, focusing the shaking on it, like a man shouting into a funnel; that the ground had moved up as hard as gravity pulls down; that a great many of the dead had died in buildings less than thirty years old, and many others under the heavy earth roofs of old ones.

I read about the old woman found alive on the eighth day, after I was out. I read about the baby found alive in her dead mother’s arms. I read the numbers, which kept changing. I read about the Arg. The engineers who had gone up the rock afterwards and measured the ruins said the citadel had been weakened, before, by things that were all very small: the clay drying out, termites, new patches of harder plaster laid onto the old softer walls in the wrong places, so that the walls couldn’t move the way old mud walls must move, a little, to survive.

I took out my notebook. It had come back to me in a parcel from the embassy in Tehran, with my passport and what was left of my bag, dug out of my room by men I never met. That is all I know of how. I opened it to the page I’d written on the wall of the castle on Christmas afternoon.
Lovely. Old. Very tired. Should be monitored.
I sat with that for a long time.
In February, when I could sit up properly, I asked a friend at the university to find me someone who could read Persian.

He brought a woman from the department of oriental studies, a lecturer, Iranian, from Shiraz, who had lived in Munich for thirty years and had a voice like Tahereh’s, deep and dry. She sat beside my bed and I gave her the little red Hafez, and she opened it to the first page, where Narges had written in English For Clara, so you can do your own fāl, and under it, in Persian, the line I couldn’t read.
The lecturer looked at it for a while. Then she looked at me over the top of her glasses.
“It isn’t Hafez,” she said. “It’s the girl’s own. Very nicely written. A schoolgirl’s hand.” She read it, first in Persian, softly, and then in German.
Khorshid hich vaqt dir nemikonad. Agar man dir kardam, montazeram bāsh.
[khor-SHEED HEECH vaght DEER ne-mee-ko-NAD. a-GAR MAN DEER kar-DAM, mon-ta-ze-RAM BAASH]
The sun is never late. If I am late, wait for me.
I said, “Wait for me.”
“Yes,” said the lecturer. “Montazeram bāsh. Wait for me. Be waiting for me.” She looked at me. “Why are you crying?”

I took the book back from her and held it shut in both hands. Outside the window the snow was still coming down on Munich, slow and grey. I thought of a girl at a kitchen table, the night before Christmas, with this cheap red book open in front of her and a pen in her hand, writing a joke for a foreigner. If I am late. She had written it laughing. I was sure of that. She had written it because she was always late and knew it, and wanted to be forgiven in advance, the way children do. She could not have known. It was only a joke about the sun. And I had waited. I had lain four days in the dark doing nothing else.
I couldn’t tell the lecturer why. But I’ve told you. You know. Don’t be sad, Clara. Wait. Someone is coming.

I had never been able to read that line. Nobody had read it to me. I had carried it under the arch for four days against my heart, in the little red book, without knowing what it said. And a voice in the dark had said it to me in English. Or I had. Or my own thirsty brain, starving and frozen, had made a girl’s voice out of the dark and put into her mouth the one thing I needed to hear, and by chance it was the thing she had written.

That’s possible. I know it is. I’ve thought about it more than about anything else in my life. I am a careful woman and a measuring woman and I know what thirst and cold and grief can do. I know that I wanted her to be there more than I’ve ever wanted anything. I know that the mind under those conditions will make what it needs out of nothing.
I also know what I heard.
I’ve stopped trying to decide between them. I think that’s allowed. I think that’s what she would say. It doesn’t tell you what will happen. It tells you what you need to hear.
From the Fault

Your people have been asking me why. They always ask me why. Every time I move, in every country, for as long as there have been people standing on me to be knocked down, the ones left standing look at the ground and ask it why.

I’ll tell you what they said here, in the tents, at the fires. And I’ll tell you what I know, from below, from twenty years after, when the tents are gone and the questions have had time to settle like dust. I won’t tell you what to think. I’m earth. I don’t think. I only remember.
They said the help was too slow.

It was. That’s simply true. The first teams with proper tools came from outside the town in the afternoon, many hours after. The government in the capital did not ask the world for help until more than half a day had passed. For the first day, the people of Bam dug each other out of me with their hands, and they saved more of each other in that first day than all the teams of all the nations of the world saved afterwards with all their dogs and machines. Your own scientists wrote that down. They wrote that in the first hours, the neighbours are the rescue, everywhere, always, and that a town that has no plan for that has no plan.
They said the rules were written and not followed.

That’s true. The book of rules existed. It had been written after Tabas and was rewritten after Bam, and is better now. But in Bam, before, hardly anyone built by it, and hardly anyone was made to, and the men whose work was to check signed papers they had not checked, sometimes for money and sometimes only because there were too many papers and not enough men. Afterwards the government said it would punish those who had built badly. I watched. I’m still watching. I didn’t see much punishment. You can’t put a whole town on trial. Everybody built like that. That was the problem.
They said the aid was stolen.

Some of it, yes. Some of it, no. People wrote about tents and blankets from abroad being sold in the bazaars; some of that was true, and some of it was goods the survivors themselves sold because they needed money more than a third blanket. A great deal more was wasted, or sat in warehouses, or arrived months late, or went to the wrong place, than was ever stolen. The money for rebuilding was promised in great amounts and came in small amounts, and each family got a sum that would not build a house, and a loan that frightened the poor. Twenty years on, nobody has added it all up and nobody will. If you want a villain in this, you will find several small ones and no large one.
They said the number of the dead was hidden.

It wasn’t hidden. It was lost. The count changed again and again: twenty-six thousand, forty-three thousand, thirty-one, thirty-four. Bodies were counted twice, in the chaos; whole families with no one left to name them went into the trenches without names; people who had come from elsewhere for work were never on any list. The number your government gives now is somewhere above thirty thousand. The real number is one only I know. I’m not going to tell you. It doesn’t matter. Every one of them was one.
They said it was a bomb. A secret test, a weapon, from America or Israel, under the desert.

It was not. I was there. I’m the only witness who was. Your scientists from many countries, some of them from countries that hate each other, measured the shaking on their instruments all over the world, and the shape of it was mine, the shape of rock sliding past rock along a crack, not the shape of a thing exploding. A bomb pushes out in all directions. I slid. Anyone who learns to read those lines on paper can see the difference, and many did, and they all agreed. The ground came straight up not because of a weapon but because the break was shallow and right underneath, and that happens, rarely, and it happened here. There was no bomb. There didn’t need to be. I was enough.

But I understand why the man in the tent needed it. I want you to understand too. A bomb has a hand behind it. A hand can be hated. A man who has lost his wife and three children in twelve seconds needs somebody to hate. He cannot hate me. I’m the ground under his feet. He has to keep standing on me.
They said it was God’s punishment for sin.

I don’t know about God. I’m earth. I can tell you that I moved under the mosque and under the opium den with the same strength, and under the house of the cleric and the house of the boy with the satellite dish, and the ones that fell were the ones built badly and the ones that stood were the ones built well, or lucky. If that’s a judgment, it’s a judgment on the steel in the roof.
They said the government knew there was a fault and told no one.

Partly. The fault to the east of the town was on the maps. People knew Bam was in country where I move. Every town in Iran is. But the branch that broke, under the houses, was not on any map. Nobody had seen it. It didn’t show itself on the surface. After Bam, your scientists went looking for hidden branches like it all over the country, and found some, and found that many of the great cities of Iran stand on top of cracks like that, which they had not drawn. That is the truest answer I can give: it was not a secret. It was a thing nobody had looked for, because looking costs money, and nobody wanted to know.
And they said, quietly, at night, the last thing. It was us. Who built your room?
You ask me who, and you ask me why, and you look for a hand in the dust and the sky: a bomb, a sin, a thief, a lie.
I am none of them. I am only I.
A hundred small hungers, each sure it was right, a bar of thin steel and a signature at night, a father who wanted his girl to have more: that is the shape of the dead on my floor.
Here is what I have learned, watching your people for a very long time.

You ask me why as if there is a single answer, a single hand, a single mistake, a single sin. There almost never is. There is the push from the south, which is mine, and has nothing to do with you. And then there are a hundred thousand small things, each of them yours, each of them reasonable on its own. A father who wanted his daughter to have a room like in the magazines. A builder who couldn’t afford the steel. An engineer who had four hundred papers to sign. A government that wrote a good book and didn’t have the will or the people to make anyone follow it. A city that grew too fast. Termites in a wall nobody had time to check. A pump that dried the clay. A man who said, at midnight, in the cold, it’s over, let’s go in.
None of them is a monster. All of them together are the shape of the dead.
You’ll want me to tell you which one is the worst. I can’t. I’m the ground. From down here, they all look the same. They all look like weight.
V. THE MOTHER WELL
22. Khesht Ayoub
I said I would tell you how I stopped smoking. I said it wasn’t brave. It wasn’t.

It was the end of June, the first summer, in the tent. Six months. The heat had come, the real heat, the Bam heat, and the tent at noon was like the inside of an oven, and we lay in it at night with the flaps open, sweating, on the hot ground. I’d been smoking every night. More than every night. I was thin. My hands shook in the morning until I had the first pipe. I’d stopped going to look at the Arg. I’d stopped going anywhere. I sat in the shade of the tent and held the pen and smoked and listened to the poem.
And one night, in the dark, Tahereh turned round.

Six months she had lain with her face to the canvas. Six months she hadn’t said a sentence to me longer than three words. That night she turned round on the mattress and lay facing me, very close, in the dark, and I could see her eyes, and she said:
“Ayoub. I lost one. I won’t lose two.”
That was all. Then she turned back.

I lay and looked at her back. Her hair had gone grey that winter. I had not noticed. I had not looked. Twenty years of marriage, and for six months I had not once looked at my wife, and in that time her hair had gone grey, and she had kept us fed, and kept the tent warm, and stood in the lines for rice, and lain every night beside a man who smelled of the pipe, and said nothing. And she had lost the same daughter. I had forgotten that. God forgive me, I had forgotten that she had lost her too. I put out my hand in the dark and did not quite touch her. I held it there, a finger’s width from her shoulder, all night.

I lay there until the sky went grey. Then I got up and went out of the tent and walked to the edge of the camp, where the desert starts, and I took the box of taryāk out of my pocket, and the pipe, my father’s pipe, sixty years old, and I dug a hole in the ground with my hands, the way I’d dug for her, and I put them in it, and I covered them over.

The next three weeks were the worst of my life, after the first morning. I won’t describe them. My body screamed for it, every hour. I shook and sweated and couldn’t eat and couldn’t sleep and lay in the tent like a dog, and Tahereh sat beside me and put wet cloths on my face, and said prayers, the same ones she’d said for Narges, steadily, out loud, the whole time, and this time I didn’t want to scream at her to stop.

And when it was over, the poem stopped. That’s what I want to tell you. When the opium went out of me, the voice reciting the poem went with it. I never heard her again. Not like that. I’ve heard her in my memory, the way anyone remembers a voice. But not in that room. That room was closed.
I’ll be honest: I missed it. I missed her voice. Some nights I still do. Some nights I’d give everything I have for one more line of it. But I had a wife.
In the autumn they started on the Arg.

The Arg had become something, after. The whole world had seen pictures of it fallen, on the news, the great mud city melted down on its rock, and it became a thing the world wanted to save. UNESCO came, the people from the United Nations who look after the great old places of the world, and put the Arg on their list, the list of the most precious places, and on another list too, of the places in danger. And money came, from Japan, from Italy, from Germany, from France, from Iran. And engineers came, and archaeologists, and conservators, and men with instruments to measure what was left, and men with drawings of what had been. And they said: we will rebuild it. Not with concrete. With earth. The old way. With khesht and kāhgel and the hands of the men of Bam.
They needed mud men. There weren’t many of us left. Some had died. Some had left. Some were in the tents with a pipe.

I went up the hill with my hands shaking, still, a little, in the mornings, and I said to the man in charge, a Tehrani with a beard and a clipboard, I made bricks for this for eleven years. I want to make them again. He looked me up and down. He’d heard about me. Bam is not big. He knew about the pipe.
“Can you still tread?” he said.
I took off my shoes.

So I made khesht again. Every day. At the foot of the rock, in the pits, the way I’d made them before, the way my father made them. Earth of Bam, water, straw, the treading, the frame, the bricks in rows in the sun. Thousands of them. Then tens of thousands. I don’t know how many, over the years. Hundreds of thousands, maybe. All of them went up onto the rock, into the walls, into the towers, slowly, a little each year, the way the Arg has always been built, the way it has always been falling.

The foreign experts came and watched us work. Japanese, Italians, Germans. They took samples of my mud and put them in little plastic bags and took them away to laboratories and came back with reports. The reports said the mud was good. I could have told them that. They asked me questions about the old ways, how my father mixed it, how long it should rest, how much straw, and I told them, and they wrote it down. A Japanese engineer, a very small, very polite man in a white helmet, spent a whole week with me at the pits, treading next to me with his trousers rolled up, laughing every time he slipped.

And they studied why the old walls had fallen. And they found what Clara had written in her notebook on Christmas afternoon: that the walls had been dry, and eaten by insects, and patched in the wrong places with harder materials that didn’t let the old mud breathe and move. They said, the new must be like the old. Soft where the old is soft. Earth with earth. They said, if you put something hard and strong into something soft and old, when the shaking comes the hard thing doesn’t bend, and the soft thing tears around it.
I listened to them say that, at a meeting, in a tent, with a projector, in English and then in Persian. And I thought about a concrete roof laid on top of an old kitchen.

I built a new house, too. Everybody had to. The government gave every family that had lost its house a little money, and a loan, and a plan, and an engineer who came to look, this time; this time they came. The new rules said: no flat concrete roofs on walls without a tie beam. Steel this thick. Foundations this deep. Inspectors. Signatures. Actual signatures, by people who had actually looked.

I built ours of brick, with a steel frame, exactly by the book. Every bar. Every beam. An inspector came four times and I followed him around with a glass of tea and he couldn’t find anything wrong, and on the fourth time he looked at me strangely and said, You’re the mud man. From the Arg. Why are you being so careful?
I said, I’m not being careful. I’m being late.
He didn’t understand. He signed.

And in the middle of the courtyard, where our old room had been, the one my grandfather built, the one that had held, I built one room the old way, like my grandfather’s. Khesht. A dome. With my own feet in the mud. For Tahereh, who would not sleep under concrete again. The inspector said it wasn’t on the plan. I said it wasn’t for the plan. He said the rules didn’t cover mud domes. I said, Then the rules don’t cover my wife. He let it go. He’d lost people too. Everybody had.
23. Return Clara
I went back for the first anniversary, December 2004. Then again the next year. Then, in 2006, for good.
Not for good. But for most of every year, for twenty years. I’ll explain.

The first time I went back, I was frightened. Not of the ground. Of the town. Of what I’d see. Of Ayoub. Of his wife, and what her face would do when she saw mine. I had a new right leg below the knee, carbon and steel, and I was still learning to trust it on uneven ground, and the whole of Bam was uneven ground. I flew to Kerman. I took the bus. The same bus, I think. The same four hours across the end of the world, the lion-coloured plain, the blue unreal mountains, the broken teahouses with their wind-catchers.

And then the bus came over the low rise, and there was the green band along the bottom of the sky, the palms, all of them, standing, exactly as they had stood, as if nothing had happened. And then the town.

It wasn’t there. That’s what I want to tell you. A year on, it still wasn’t there. The rubble had been cleared from the main roads and bulldozed into heaps. And in its place, in every direction, in long white rows, there were tents and boxes. The camps. White canvas and pale metal, thousands of them, laid out on the bare earth in a grid. Laundry hanging between them. Children running between them. Smoke from cooking fires. And among them, here and there, the first new buildings going up, brick and steel, square, with scaffolding.
And on its rock, the Arg. A heap. With scaffolding on it.

They were waiting for me at the bus station. Both of them. Ayoub, and Tahereh, standing a little apart from the crowd, in their coats. I got off the bus and stood there with my bag and my new leg and my heart going and didn’t know what to do.

It was Tahereh who moved. She came straight to me, across the dust, and took my face in her two hands, the way the women had at Yalda, and looked at me for a long time, close. Her eyes were very tired. Then she kissed me, once on each cheek and then a third time, which is what you do in Iran for someone who is family.
She said something in Persian. Ayoub translated, in English. He had more English now. More than forty words.
“She says, you came back for her.”
“Tell her yes.”
He told her. She nodded. She didn’t let go of my face.
Then she let go, and stepped back, and looked me up and down, very closely, the way she had looked at my hand on Yalda night, and her eyes stopped at my right leg, and she said something sharp.
“She says,” said Ayoub, “the earth took a piece of you too. Good. Now you are from Bam.”

That Yalda we spent in their box. Two metres by three, with a door and a window, in a row of boxes in the camp at the edge of town. We couldn’t all fit inside. So they put a carpet on the ground outside the door and a cloth on the carpet and the food on the cloth, and we sat on the ground under the stars in our coats, the three of us, and their neighbour’s family, and the families from the next boxes, maybe twenty people, the way it had been. Pomegranates. Watermelon, kept since summer. Dates. Tea. Not much else. Nobody had much. It didn’t matter.

Nobody told stories that year. Nobody did a magic trick. Nobody told about the snow. We just sat together in the cold, the longest night, keeping each other company until morning, which is what it was always for. That’s what I understood that night, that I hadn’t understood the first time. It isn’t a party. It was never a party. It’s a vigil. You stay awake together in the dark so that nobody has to get through it alone.
Near midnight, Tahereh said, “The book.”

Ayoub went into the box and came back with it. The green book. Narges’s book, her great-grandmother’s. Its cloth cover was stained now, darker on one corner, and there was dust still in the creases of its spine that would never come out. He had found it himself, in the spring, when the machines came to clear the lot where her room had been. It had been under the slab, by her bed, all that time.
He sat down on the carpet beside me. And he held the book out, not to me, but to Tahereh.
“For me,” he said, in English, so I’d understand. “Fāl. For me. This year.”
Tahereh took it. She held it in her lap. She closed her eyes and said the little prayer under her breath. O Hafez of Shiraz. And she opened it with her thumb, anywhere, without looking.
It fell open at the same page.

I saw it. I knew the shape of the lines on the page, even though I couldn’t read them. I’d looked at Narges’s copy of that poem every day for a year. Tahereh looked down. She didn’t read it aloud. She didn’t need to. She just turned the book round, in her lap, and showed it to Ayoub. And Ayoub looked at it, and then he looked up at the sky, at all those stars, and laughed. Once. Not a happy laugh. Not an unhappy one either.
“Of course,” he said, in English. And then he said something to me I’ve thought about ever since.
“A book,” he said, “opens where it has been opened most.”
I said, “Yes.”

“That’s the earth,” he said. “That’s mud. That’s a road. That’s a crack in a wall. Things go where they have gone before.” He touched the page. “She opened this one, every night, the last year. A hundred times. So now it opens here. That’s all.” He paused. “That’s not a miracle.”
“No.”
He closed the book. He held it on his knees.
“But it isn’t nothing,” he said.
24. The Mother Well Ayoub

The guesthouse was rebuilt in 2007. Not by the old owner, the man with the grey beard. His wife had died under it, and he didn’t want to stay. He went to live with his son in Shiraz. A man from Kerman bought the land and built a new guesthouse there, with a steel frame, by the book, with a courtyard and a pool, and he planted a new orange tree, because the old one, which had survived the earthquake, had died the next summer of thirst, when the qanat under the town stopped running for a while.

But the steps were still there. The pāyāb. The stairs in the corner of the courtyard, going down into the dark, cut into the ground. The new owner kept them. He put a little gate across the top, and a lamp, and a sign in Persian and English that said Historic Water Stair, 17th Century, which made me laugh, because the steps were probably older, and because nobody had ever thought they were historic until a German woman lay at the top of them for four days.

The qanat came back too. The muqanni came, three of them, old men from the villages, with their buckets and their ropes and their white shirts, and the government paid them, and the foreigners paid them, and they went down into the tunnels that had collapsed in the earthquake and dug them out again, the way muqanni have always dug, by hand, by lamp, in the dark. It took them three years.

I went down with them. I want you to know that. Fifty-four years old, my knees already going, and I broke my father’s oath to my mother on the first morning the muqanni rigged their windlass over the shaft in the garden where I’d gone down on the fourth night. The oldest of them, a man from a village near Kerman with a white beard to his chest, looked at me, and at my hands, and asked who had taught me. I told him the name of my grandfather’s partner. He was quiet for a moment. Then he handed me a white shirt.

So I learned it properly, at last, late in my life, in the dark, on my knees, with a short pick and a lamp. I learned to read the roof by tapping it and listening. I learned to set the clay hoops, the kaval, one against the next, where the earthquake had cracked the soft earth and it was trying to close. I learned to clear a collapse from the downstream side so that the water could go on running past my legs while I worked. I learned the flame before the foot, again, with my life on it this time. And every evening I came up the shaft on the rope into the red sun, grey from head to foot, with my white shirt brown, and Clara, who had come back that spring to work on the Arg, was standing at the windlass with the boys from the camp, turning the charkh, hauling up my buckets of earth, laughing at how heavy they were.

Some of the qanats under Bam never came back. Some did. Ours did. The one under the old town, the one that ran past the old man’s shaft, and under the guesthouse, and down to the gardens below the Arg.
In the spring of 2008 I took Clara down to it.

She’d been working on the Arg for two years by then, with the Germans, in the part of the citadel the experts had given them. The stables. The same stables where I’d been working the first day she came up the hill and put her hand in my mud. She came every October and stayed till the heat drove her out in June. She spoke Persian now, badly, with that accent, the gh too soft and the kh too hard. She lived in a rented room in the new town. She ate at our house on Fridays. Tahereh taught her to cook fesenjān and to swear.
That April evening, after work, we went to the new guesthouse, and the new owner, who knew the story, opened the little gate for us with a bow, and we went down the steps.

She went slowly, with her hand on the wall, putting her new foot down carefully on each worn step. I went in front, backwards, with the torch, the way you’d go down a ladder with a child above you. Fifteen steps. Twenty. The light from the courtyard became a white square, then a coin. Then we were at the bottom, crouching, in the low passage, in the cold old air, and at our feet, in its channel, the water.
Running. Clear as air. Out of the dark on the left, into the dark on the right. Cold enough to hurt your bones. Going home.

We sat on the bottom step for a long time with our feet near the water. I turned off the torch. It was very dark and very quiet. The drop was still falling somewhere up the tunnel, slow, like a clock. It had been falling the whole time. Through all of it.
I want to tell you what I said to her, in the dark, because it’s the closest I’ve come to understanding anything, and because I said it in Persian and she understood every word.
I said: I’ve been angry at the earth.

I said: For four years. Every day. Making bricks out of it. Standing on it. Burying my mother’s friends in it. My daughter. I’ve been treading it with my feet every morning like I was treading on its face.

I said: And it doesn’t care. That’s the thing. It doesn’t care that I’m angry. It didn’t care when it took her. It didn’t do it to me. It doesn’t know my name. It was full, so it let go. That’s all. It’s like being angry at the water for running downhill.

I said: Down here, I can feel that. Up there, I can’t. Up there there’s a room I built, and an inspector, and a government, and a book of rules, and aid that didn’t come, and a man in a tent who thinks it was a bomb, and a cleric who thinks it was God, and me, who thinks it was me. Up there it’s all hands. Everybody looking for the hand.

I said: Down here there’s no hand. There’s just the mother. Going home. The same way she went home before there was a Bam, and the same way she’ll go home after there isn’t one. She gives you the water, and she gives you the crack, and they’re the same gift, and she doesn’t apologise for either.
Clara didn’t say anything for a while. Then she reached across in the dark and found my hand, the way I’d found hers through the gap in the bricks, and held it.
“Gham makhor,” she said. With that accent.
“I’m trying,” I said.
“I know.”
“Narges would have said it better.”
“Narges,” Clara said, “would have said you’re being very dramatic, Baba. We are a dramatic people.”

I laughed. In the dark, at the bottom of the stairs, beside the water. It was the first time I had laughed, really laughed, since Yalda. It went off down the tunnel and came back to us off the old walls, the way the poem had, and the water took it, and carried it away, going home.
25. Looking Back Clara

I’m writing this in Bam, in December 2025. I’m fifty-six. I’ve been coming here for twenty-two years. It’s the twentieth of December, and tomorrow is Yalda, and I’m sitting in my rented room in the new town with the window open, and I can see the Arg on its rock from my desk.
It’s standing.

Not all of it. Not as it was. It will never be as it was; nothing is. But the great outer wall is back, most of it, with its towers. The gates. Many of the houses and lanes inside the walls, built up again in khesht and kāhgel, by hand, the old way. The stables, my stables, done. The castle at the top, the governor’s citadel, is still being raised. They’ve been working on it for twenty years. They’ll be working on it for twenty more. The square tower isn’t back yet. Every winter I look up from my desk at the place on the sky where it should be, and every winter there’s a little more of it. In 2013 the people at UNESCO took the Arg off their list of places in danger. It’s still on the other list, the list of the most precious places in the world. It belongs there.
In the evenings, it still changes colour. Gold, then orange, then red, then that strange soft violet, and then the light goes out of it all at once. Ayoub was right. You don’t get tired of it.

I said I’d tell you, before I finished, what became of the things people said. In the tents. At the fires. I’ve had twenty-two years to watch. Here’s what I’ve seen. I’ll try to be fair. I’m a measuring woman. I’ll measure.

The help was too slow. That was true, and it’s been studied, and written up in report after report, and the lesson every report draws is the same: in the first day, the neighbours are the rescue. Iran has trained more people since, in towns all over the country, in how to dig, how to listen, how to lift. Whether that would be enough, the next time, nobody knows. There will be a next time. Everybody here knows that.

The rules were not followed. That was true. After Bam the rules were made stricter, and in Bam itself, during the rebuilding, they were followed, mostly, because everybody was watching. The new town is built well. I’ve been inside a hundred of its houses. I’ve looked at the steel. Elsewhere in Iran, people tell me, it’s better than it was, and not as good as it should be. That’s what people tell me about every country.

The aid was stolen. Some was. Some wasn’t. More was wasted. Nobody ever added it up. I went looking for a thief and found a few greedy men, a great many tired ones, and warehouses full of blankets that arrived in the spring.

The number was hidden. It wasn’t hidden; it was lost. The official count went up and down for years and settled, finally, somewhere above thirty thousand. Some researchers think it was more. Nobody will ever know exactly. There are rows in the cemetery at the edge of the desert where the photographs are missing, because there was nobody left to come and look.

It was a bomb. It was not. Every seismologist who looked, from every country, including countries that agreed on nothing else, said the same thing: the shaking had the shape of a fault slipping, not of an explosion. That was settled within weeks. The rumour never died. It comes back, every time the ground moves in Iran. In October 2024, after a small earthquake in the north, the internet filled up overnight with people saying it had been a secret bomb test, and seismologists had to stand up and say again, patiently, that it was not. I’ve stopped being angry about it. I understand it now. I’ve sat by those fires. A bomb has a hand behind it.

The government knew about the fault. They knew about the one on the map. They didn’t know about the one underneath. After Bam, scientists went looking for hidden faults like it, under other cities, and found that a great many of Iran’s cities stand on them, unseen, unmapped, including Tehran. They’re mapping them now. Slowly. It costs money.

It was us. That was the hardest thing anybody said at the fires, and it was the truest. A great many of the people who died in Bam died in new buildings built badly by people who loved them. Ayoub said it first and he said it most. I’ve never once heard him say it about anyone but himself.
And the voice.

I’ve thought about it for twenty-two years. I’ve read everything. I’ve read about what thirst does, and cold, and the dark, and grief. I’ve talked to doctors. I’ve talked to other people who were buried, in other earthquakes, in Turkey, in Pakistan, in Italy. Many of them heard voices. Some heard the dead. Some heard God. One man in Turkey heard his mother singing a song she used to sing when he was small, and she was alive, two hundred kilometres away, asleep in her bed.

I know the voice could have come from me. From my own starving brain in the dark, building a girl out of the poem I’d heard once by lamplight and the two words she taught me and the need I had for someone to be there. I know that’s the likeliest answer. I’m a careful woman. I believe in the likeliest answer.

I also know that the voice said Wait, in English, the one thing she had written in my book in a language I couldn’t read. And that I waited. And that someone came, through the earth, three nights later, saying her poem.

I’ve stopped trying to make those two things fit together. They don’t. They lie next to each other, the way the two sides of a fault lie next to each other, touching all along their length, and not moving, and not becoming one thing, until one day they do.

The qanats, too, I should tell you about, because he would want me to. In 2016, UNESCO put the Persian qanat on its list of the most precious places in the world: eleven of them, from all over Iran, chosen to stand for all the rest. Two of the eleven are here, a couple of kilometres south of the Arg, near the village of Baravat [ba-raa-VAT]. One of them is the qanat Ayoub’s grandfather died in. Ayoub went to the little ceremony in his good suit and stood at the back and didn’t say anything to anybody, and on the way home in the car he cried, once, briefly, and then said that the speeches had been too long.

But the list hasn’t saved them. Nothing has. All over Iran the pumps go on drawing the water under the desert down, lower every year, and the old qanats go on running thinner, and some of them stop. There are still muqanni. Not many, and most of them old. The young men still drive taxis in Kerman. There are people trying to bring the old tunnels back, here and elsewhere, with money from the government and from abroad, and some of the tunnels have come back, and the water runs in them again, and the gardens at their mouths are green. It is slow. It is always slow. Ayoub says it takes about as long to save a qanat as it takes to dig one, which is about as long as a man’s life.

Ayoub is seventy-four. He still makes khesht for the Arg. Not every day now. His knees. He still takes off his shoes and treads it, though, every morning he works, and the young men on the crew watch him and try to copy his feet. He still drops the ball of mud from his shoulder onto the stone to test it. It still lands like a tired man sitting down.
His English is good now. Better than my Persian. We’ve been doing something together, for twenty years, at his kitchen table on Fridays, with the green pen.
We’ve been translating the poem.

Narges’s poem. The one from the fāl. Hafez’s Yusof-e gomgashteh. Her own translation was only four lines, in her round careful hand, on the folded page she gave me on the longest night. Ayoub found the rest of her attempt in a school notebook, in the spring, under the slab, and it was only a few more lines, crossed out, rewritten, crossed out again, with question marks in the margin. Stranger’s coat?? she had written next to one line.

So we finished it. He brings the Persian and what it means in his bones. I bring the English and what it sounds like in the ear. We argue about every word. Tahereh brings tea and tells us we’re both wrong. It has taken us twenty years to do ten lines, which, Ayoub says, is quick, for a qanat.
It’s finished now. It’s not good. It’s a stranger wearing his coat. But it’s warm.
We’re going to read it tomorrow night. At Yalda. To the family.
26. Gham Makhor Ayoub
Yalda. The twenty-first of December, 2025. Twenty-two years.

My house is full. My sisters, old women now, with their husbands, older. Their children, who were the little ones doing the coin trick, with children of their own. Our neighbour and his wife and their sons, who are grown men, and their wives. Tahereh’s brother from Kerman. Clara. And Tahereh, my wife, who is cleverer than me and no longer pretends otherwise. Twenty-six people.

We sit in the dome. Tahereh’s dome, the one I built her in the middle of the courtyard so that she would never have to sleep under concrete again. Khesht, kāhgel, my feet in the mud, twenty years ago. It’s the coolest room in summer and the warmest in winter and the strongest shape God made. We spread the cloth on the carpet. The pomegranates broken open in the glass bowl, red, shining. The watermelon, kept since summer, cut in great wedges. Dates. Bam dates, the black soft ones, that taste like honey that has been sad for a long time and has finally been forgiven. Tea. More tea.

We tell stories. My uncle is dead, God rest him, but his son tells the story about the donkey and the mullah, worse than his father did, and everyone laughs at the same places. A great-nephew does the trick with the coin, and it goes wrong, and everyone laughs. Somebody tells about the snow that came to Bam when my eldest sister was a girl, the only time, and the palms standing in the white with their heads bent like old men praying, and somebody’s father going out to throw a snowball at the mosque. It was our father. Nobody says so any more. It’s everybody’s father now. That’s what happens to a story.
Near midnight, my sister says, “The book.”

I get up and go to the niche in the wall and take it down. The green book. Narges’s book. It’s falling apart now. Clara has done what she can to it; she’s a conservator, after all; she’s sewn the spine, and made a box for it, a beautiful little box of wood that she says is the way her father would have made it. The dust is still in the creases. Clara says it would take the paper with it, if she tried to get it out. So it stays. The dust of Bam. The earth of my bricks.

I don’t open it. Not tonight. Tonight I take out of my pocket a folded sheet of paper, the one Clara and I finished last month, at the kitchen table, with the green pen, and I unfold it, and I stand in the middle of Tahereh’s dome, in the lamplight, in front of twenty-six people who loved my daughter, and I read it, in English, with my terrible accent, the poem that was her fāl for a stranger on the longest night of the year.

I’m not going to give you the whole of it. It’s not good enough. It’s ours. I’ll give you the four lines that were hers, the ones she wrote out for Clara on the longest night, that we didn’t change, because they were already right:
Lost Joseph will come home to Canaan. Do not grieve.
The hut of sorrows will one day be a garden of roses. Do not grieve.
If the flood of nothing comes and pulls up the root of everything that is, while Noah is the captain of your ship, do not grieve.
When I finish, nobody says anything for a long time. Then Tahereh, beside me, puts her hand on my arm, and says, in Persian, “Khub bud [KHOOB bood].” It was good.
It wasn’t good. It’s a stranger in a coat. But she says it was good, and she’s cleverer than me, so it was good.
At dawn, the way we always do, we go out to greet the sun.

We go up onto the roof of the new house. It’s flat. Concrete. A tie beam all the way round, with steel inside it as thick as my thumb, signed by an inspector who looked at it four times. It is the strongest roof in this street. I built it myself. I still don’t trust it, and I go up on it every morning anyway, because you have to stand on something.

From up there you can see the whole of Bam. The new town, square and pale, with its water tanks and its washing. The palms, millions of them, standing, the way they always stand. The desert, gold, going out to the mountains in the south, which are white on top this morning with snow. The lines of craters running across the desert from the mountains, where the qanats go down to their mothers. And on its rock, the Arg, coming up out of the dark grey of the morning, walls and towers, the colour of the desert, the desert standing up.

And then the sun comes over the mountains. Red. Enormous. The way it has always come up over Bam. The light runs across the desert and up the rock and touches the top of the citadel, the place where the square tower was, where the scaffolding is, where the young men will be treading mud tomorrow morning with their trousers rolled up, trying to copy my feet. Gold.

Clara is standing beside me. Fifty-six, with her new leg and her grey hair under a blue scarf, tied badly, slipping. She’s waited a long time to watch the sun come up over the Arg with someone. Twenty-two years. She’s never once said so.
Just before the light reaches the rock, she says something, very quietly, in her bad Persian, not to me.
“Dir kardi [DEER kar-DEE].” You’re late.

I don’t say anything. I know who she means. I look at the place on the roof beside her where a tall thin girl in a long coat would stand, if she had come, out of breath, laughing, with her scarf slipping and an excuse ready. There is nobody there. There is only the cold, and the light coming.
“Then we wait,” I say.
She nods. We wait. The sun is never late. It comes.
Every day from now is longer. That’s the whole point.
I put my hand over my heart, on the left, over the inside pocket of my coat, where the green pen is, buttoned in.
Gham makhor, I say, to nobody. To the earth. To the sun.
Don’t eat sorrow.
I’m trying.
From the Mother Well
Let me tell you about the mother.

Up in the hills south of Bam, at the head of every qanat, there is a well. The first one dug. The deepest. The one that reached the water. Your people call it the mother well, the mādar-chāh, and they are right to. Everything downhill of it lives on what comes out of it. The tunnel, the gardens, the palms, the town, the people, the girl reading poems by lamplight, the man treading mud with his feet: all of it is the mother’s child. She doesn’t see them. She’s too deep. She only gives what comes down to her from the mountain, and she lets it go downhill, and she has done this for longer than any of the names in your books.

I am the mother. Not the well. The ground the well was dug into. I am every mother well in this land and every crack the water rises through. I am the thing that gave you Bam and the thing that took it away, and I want you to understand at last, before I stop speaking, that these were never two different things. The water comes up where I am broken. The oasis grows along the fault. Your ancestors didn’t know that, and they built on it anyway, and if they had known they would have built on it anyway, because the water was there, and you go where the water is. That is the oldest bargain. It’s still the only one.
You want me to apologise.

All of you. I hear it under every question you ask me. Why Bam. Why so many. Why my daughter. Why the new room and not the old one. Under every why there’s another word, the one you really want, and it’s sorry. You want the ground to say sorry.

I can’t. Not because I’m cruel. Because I’m not anything. I’m older than sorry. Sorry is a thing that happens between people, between two who could have chosen differently. I’ve never chosen anything. I’m pushed from the south a finger’s width a year and I fold and I crack and I hold and I let go, and I have done it since before there was a sky over this desert, and I will do it after the last brick of the last city has gone back into me. I don’t do it to you. I barely know you’re there.

But I know you’ve changed me. That’s the thing I’ve come to say. In the time you’ve been on me, a short time, a match struck in a dark room, you’ve changed me more than all the ages before. You’ve drilled me and pumped me dry. You’ve poured me into moulds and burned me and made me hard. You’ve laid lids of stone on top of soft walls. You’ve built cities in every crease where I give you water, and filled them with millions, and gone on building, faster, higher, heavier, without looking down. You’ve changed how I fall. Not when. How. When I let go now, I take more of you than I ever took before, and it’s not because I’ve grown angrier. It’s because you’ve grown heavier, and you built yourselves out of things that don’t forgive.

I am not your enemy. I’m what you’re standing on. I evolve with you, whether either of us likes it. You make me drier and I crack more easily. You make me harder and I break more cruelly. You forget me and I remind you.

Here is what I have learned, from the mud man and the German woman, from the girl who read poems, from the girl’s mother, who would not sleep under concrete again, from the thirty thousand who went back into me in twelve seconds one morning after the longest night.

You can’t own me. Not with a book of rules. Not with steel as thick as your thumb. Not with prayer, not with money, not with a list of the world’s precious places, not with satellites. You can prepare. You must prepare. Build soft where I’m soft. Tie your roofs to your walls. Look for my hidden cracks before you build on them, and when you find one, don’t pretend you didn’t. Train your neighbours to dig. All of that matters. All of that will save some of you, next time, and there will be a next time.
But underneath all of it, you have to do the thing your people are worst at. You have to surrender.

Not to despair. Not to give up. Surrender the way the palm does. The palm survived. Every one in Bam. It has no bones to break. It doesn’t fight the shaking. It bends. It lets the ground do what the ground does, and it stands up straight again after. The mud man understood this, at the bottom of the stairs, in the dark, beside the water. That there is no hand. That there’s only the mother, going home, the way she always goes. That the most you can ever do is build well, and love hard, and stay awake together through the longest night, and greet the sun when it comes back, and not expect anything to apologise.
I don’t apologise.

I keep everything. The bricks of the citadel. The roof of the white room. The girl, in her coat, with the dust of my body on her eyelashes. The man in the tent who thought it was a bomb. His wife and three children. The thirty thousand. They are all in me now, all of them, in the cold, in the dark, under the town, beside the water. Nothing is lost here. Only buried.

And every spring the snow melts on the mountains to the south, and sinks into me, and runs down in the dark through my cracks to the mother well, and the mother lets it go, downhill, through the tunnel, under the old town and under the new one, past the stairs where the German woman lay, and out into the gardens, where the palms drink it, and the oranges, and the dates, the black soft ones, that taste of honey that has been sad for a long time and has finally been forgiven.
Your people will eat them at Yalda, on the longest night, and stay awake together until the sun comes back.
I have sung to you four times between the chapters of this story. If you keep nothing else of mine, keep this. It is all of them in one, the way the town is all of its bricks.
Wet me and tread me and lay me in the sun;
I’ll hold up your roof till the holding is done.
Where the water comes up, there the rock has been split: the gift and the grave have one root under it.
I held my breath for a thousand years and let it go in twelve. Keep your tears.
A hundred small hungers, a roof like a lid:
I don’t know the hand. I know what it did.
So bend like the palm when the ground starts to sway, stay up together till night turns to day;
I keep what comes down to me, every last one.
I don’t apologise. Look. Here is the sun.
That’s all I have to give you. It has always been enough.

GLOSSARY
ājil [aa-JEEL] — Persian. A mixture of nuts and dried fruit eaten on festive nights.
Āmrikā [aam-ree-KAA] — Persian, America.
anār [a-NAAR] — Persian, pomegranate. Eaten at Yalda for its red seeds, the colour of dawn and of life.
Ardashir [ar-da-SHEER] — The first king of the Sasanian dynasty of Persia, who in the Shahnameh kills the worm of Kerman.
Arg [ARG] — Persian, citadel. The Arg-e Bam [ARG-eh BAM] is the walled earthen city on the rock above Bam, the largest building made of mud brick in the world.
Ayoub [a-YOOB] — Persian and Arabic, Job, the prophet tested by the loss of everything he had. The narrator who makes bricks.
Sabr-e Ayoub [SABR-eh a-YOOB], the patience of Job, is a
Persian saying for long suffering without complaint.
azizam [a-zee-ZAM] — Persian, my dear.
Bā-ādam [baa-AA-dam] — Persian, a real person; someone decent and genuine.
Baba [BAA-baa] — Persian, dad.
Bam [BAM] — An oasis town in Kerman province, southeastern
Iran, on the edge of the Lut desert.
Baravat [ba-raa-VAT] — A village just south of Bam, beside two of the qanats on UNESCO’s list.
bokhor [bo-KHOR] — Persian, eat.
charkh [CHARKH] — Persian, wheel. The wooden windlass turned at the top of a qanat shaft to haul up earth.
dalv [DALV] — Persian, bucket. The leather bucket used to lift spoil out of a qanat.
fāl [FAAL] — Persian, fortune, omen. The fāl-e Hāfez [FAAL-eh haa-FEZ] is the custom of opening the poems of Hafez at random to read one’s fortune.
fenjān [fen-JAAN] — Persian, cup. A copper bowl with a hole in it, floated in water to measure each family’s turn of qanat water by time.
Ferdowsi [fer-dow-SEE] — The poet who wrote the Shahnameh about a thousand years ago.
fesenjān [fe-sen-JAAN] — Persian. A stew of chicken, ground walnuts and pomegranate syrup.
gham makhor [GHAM ma-KHOR] — Persian, don’t grieve; literally don’t eat sorrow. The refrain of the Hafez poem in this book.
Gonabad [go-naa-BAAD] — A town in northeastern Iran with one of the oldest and deepest qanats.
Hafez [haa-FEZ] — The poet of Shiraz, who died more than six hundred years ago and whose poems nearly every Iranian knows by heart.
Haftvād [haft-VAAD] — In the Shahnameh, the poor man of Kerman whose daughter found a worm in an apple.
Helāl-e Ahmar [he-LAAL-eh AH-mar] — Persian, Red Crescent.
Iran’s disaster relief society.
hendevāneh [hen-de-vaa-NEH] — Persian, watermelon. Kept from summer to be eaten at Yalda.
Isā [ee-SAA] — Persian and Arabic, Jesus.
kāhgel [kaah-GEL] — Persian, straw-mud. A plaster of mud and chopped straw smoothed over earthen walls.
kaval [ka-VAAL] — Persian. Oval rings of baked clay set end to end to line a qanat tunnel through soft earth.
Kerman [ker-MAAN] — The province and its capital city in southeastern Iran, about three hours from Bam.
khesht [KHESHT] — Persian, mud brick. Earth mixed with water and straw, shaped in a frame and dried in the sun.
Lehm [LAYM] — German, clay, loam. The earth used for building in old German farmhouses.
Lut [LOOT] — The desert east of Bam, one of the hottest places on
Earth.
mādar-chāh [maa-DAR chaah] — Persian, mother well. The first and deepest well at the head of a qanat, where it reaches the water.
manqal [man-GHAL] — Persian. A small brazier of glowing charcoal.
mazāfati [ma-zaa-fa-TEE] — Persian. The soft, black, very sweet dates of Bam.
mazhar [MAZ-har] — Persian, place of appearing. Where a qanat’s water comes out of the ground.
mehmān [meh-MAAN] — Persian, guest. A guest is a gift from God. merci [mer-SEE] — From French, thank you. The everyday Persian way of saying thanks.
mirāb [meer-AAB] — Persian, master of water. The man who divides a qanat’s water among its owners.
muqanni [mo-GHAN-nee] — Persian, qanat digger. The men who dig and repair qanats by hand.
Narges [nar-GES] — Persian, narcissus, the flower that blooms in the Iranian winter. Ayoub’s daughter.
pāyāb [paa-YAAB] — Persian. A stairway cut down from a house or garden to the water of a qanat.
qanat [gha-NAAT] — Persian. An underground tunnel, dug by hand on a very gentle slope, that carries water from the foot of the mountains to the surface far away, with no pump.
qātel [ghaa-TEL] — Persian, murderer. What the muqanni call the qanat among themselves.
shahid [sha-HEED] — Persian and Arabic, martyr.
Shahnameh [shaah-naa-MEH] — Persian, the Book of Kings.
Ferdowsi’s epic of the old kings of Iran.
Shakh-e Nabat [SHAAKH-eh na-BAAT] — Persian, branch of rock candy. The name of the woman Hafez loved, invoked when opening his book.
Shiraz [shee-RAAZ] — The city in southern Iran where Hafez lived and is buried.
Tahereh [taa-heh-REH] — Persian, pure. Ayoub’s wife.
taryāk [tar-YAAK] — Persian, opium.
vāfur [vaa-FOOR] — Persian. A long clay pipe for smoking opium.
Yalda [YAL-daa] — Persian. The longest night of the year, around
December 21, when families stay up together until dawn.
Yusof [yoo-SOF] — Persian and Arabic, Joseph. The lost son who comes home in the Hafez poem.
